# Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-Set Diffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks

Rodrigo Casado Noguerales^(1,2,$`*`$) Dimitri von Rütte¹ Bernhard
Schölkopf^(1,2,3) Thomas Hofmann¹ Aran Raoufi¹ ¹ETH Zurich ²Max Planck
Institute for Intelligent Systems ³ELLIS Institute Tübingen

###### Abstract

Discrete diffusion models iteratively denoise a noisy sequence of
categorical data such as text, enabling any-order generation with
self-correction and in-filling capabilities. This makes them promising
candidates for reasoning, planning, and constrained-generation tasks
like coding and math. Yet masked and uniform diffusion erase a token’s
identity in a single corruption event, so their noisy states cannot
explicitly represent partially resolved uncertainty in which several
alternatives remain plausible. We close this gap with Binary Discrete
Diffusion, a family of continuous-time discrete-diffusion processes
whose noisy state is a set of candidate tokens per position, represented
as a binary membership vector. Binary diffusion changes candidate sets
through additions and removals, allowing information to be lost and
recovered gradually while the diffusion state itself represents partial
uncertainty. On Sudoku-Extreme, Boxoban, and graph coloring, the
symmetric formulation of binary diffusion consistently outperforms
strong, well-tuned masked and uniform baselines under matched
architectures and controlled training, sampling, and tuning budgets,
with its largest gains on the hardest instances, while remaining
competitive on language modeling (Text8, TinyStories, OpenWebText).
These results support candidate sets as an effective intermediate
representation for iterative reasoning and show that the corruption
kernel can materially change the computation learned by the reverse
model.

## 1 Introduction

Discrete diffusion models generate by iteratively refining a corrupted
sequence. Unlike autoregressive generation, decisions need not follow a
fixed left-to-right order and can be revised later, while many positions
can be updated in parallel ([Schiff et al., 2025](#bib.bib45); [Sahoo
et al., 2024](#bib.bib40); [Gong et al., 2025](#bib.bib19)). These
properties make discrete diffusion attractive for reasoning, planning,
and constrained generation ([Ye et al., 2025](#bib.bib62); [Wewer
et al., 2025](#bib.bib60)). Yet sample quality at finite inference
budgets remains challenging, motivating work on ordering, remasking,
planned denoising, and search ([Kim et al., 2025](#bib.bib27); [Wang
et al., 2025b](#bib.bib58); [Liu et al., 2025](#bib.bib30); [Bai et al.,
2026](#bib.bib3)). We instead focus on a complementary axis: the
corruption process itself. How much can be gained by changing the
corruption process, and in particular the intermediate representation on
which denoising operates? Logic and planning are useful testbeds: they
impose global constraints, admit exact solve-rate evaluation, and scale
cleanly in difficulty at manageable computational cost, while sharing
structure with coding, mathematics, and biological design ([Sahoo
et al., 2026](#bib.bib42); [Avdeyev et al., 2023](#bib.bib2); [Stärk
et al., 2024](#bib.bib51)). They also expose a mismatch in the dominant
masked and uniform kernels ([Sahoo et al., 2024](#bib.bib40); [Shi
et al., 2024](#bib.bib48); [Schiff et al., 2025](#bib.bib45); [Sahoo
et al., 2025](#bib.bib41)): a position cannot naturally express that
several alternatives remain plausible. A model solving Sudoku, for
example, might narrow a cell from $`\{2,7,9\}`$ to $`\{7,9\}`$, later
reopen $`2`$ as neighboring decisions are revised, and eventually settle
on $`7`$.

We propose to make such candidate sets themselves the diffusion states.
A clean token is a singleton, while during reverse generation
intermediate states can carry several live hypotheses that may be
eliminated or restored. More broadly, the corruption kernel does more
than specify how examples are noised: it determines what information
survives at intermediate times and how the model’s prediction is
translated into reverse moves and their rates. Identical architectures
can therefore induce qualitatively different iterative computations
under different kernels. We instantiate this idea with Binary Discrete
Diffusion, representing candidate sets by binary membership vectors in
$`\{0,1\}^{V}`$
(Figure [1](#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")).
In binary symmetric diffusion, membership bits can switch both on and
off, allowing hypotheses to be eliminated and later restored. In binary
absorbing diffusion, corruption only adds candidates, so reverse
generation progressively prunes the set toward a singleton.

Although each position has a nominal state space of size $`2^{V}`$,
every state has only $`V`$ single-bit neighbors, and all neighboring
reverse rates can be computed in $`O(V)`$ time from the model’s usual
$`V`$-way prediction, without enumerating subsets. The model learns
these dynamics from clean solutions without candidate labels,
task-specific deduction rules, or symbolic search. The richer state also
enables candidate-aware sampling: we derive exact ancestral updates
through a shared clean-token proposal, adapt re-corrupt sampling, and,
building on $`\Psi`$-sampling and confidence-guided
remasking ([Deschenaux et al., 2026](#bib.bib12); [Wang et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib58)), develop revision rules that choose both _which
positions_ to reconsider and _which hypotheses_ to reopen.

We evaluate Binary Discrete Diffusion on Sudoku-Extreme ([Wang et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib57)), Boxoban ([Guez et al., 2018](#bib.bib21)), and
graph coloring under controlled architectures, training budgets, and
sampler tuning, using direct single-attempt solutions without
verifier-guided selection. Across all three tasks, a consistent pattern
emerges: binary symmetric diffusion outperforms uniform diffusion, and
both outperform masked and binary absorbing diffusion. The advantage of
binary symmetric over uniform grows on harder regimes, including
low-clue Sudoku, long-horizon Boxoban, and graph coloring far beyond the
training size. On Text8, TinyStories, and OpenWebText ([Mahoney,
2011](#bib.bib32); [Eldan & Li, 2023](#bib.bib13); [Gokaslan & Cohen,
2019](#bib.bib18)), binary diffusion remains competitive with
established kernels. These results support candidate sets as an
effective intermediate representation for iterative reasoning and show
that the corruption process can materially change the computation
learned by the reverse model.

## 2 Discrete diffusion modeling

We consider a data distribution $`p_{\mathrm{data}}`$ on sequences of
length $`L`$ over a finite vocabulary $`[V]=\{1,\ldots,V\}`$. Starting
from $`Z_{0}\sim p_{\mathrm{data}}`$, we corrupt its positions
independently with a continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC)
$`Z_{t}=(Z_{t}^{1},\ldots,Z_{t}^{L})`$, whose distribution approaches an
easily sampled noise distribution as $`t\uparrow 1`$. We write
$`q_{t\mid s}(y\mid z)`$ for the one-position transition distribution or
_kernel_ between times $`s<t`$ and states $`z,y`$. For masked and
uniform diffusion we use ([Austin et al., 2021](#bib.bib1))

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
q_{t\mid 0}(y\mid c)=\begin{cases}(1-t)\mathbf{1}\{y=c\}+t\mathbf{1}\{y=\mathtt{m}\},&\text{masked},\\
(1-t)\mathbf{1}\{y=c\}+t/V,&\text{uniform}.\end{cases}
``` |  | (1) |

Thus $`Z_{t}`$ can be sampled directly at any time $`t`$, without
simulating the intervening jumps.

We write $`Q_{t}(z,y)`$ for the forward jump rate from $`z`$ to $`y`$,
so that $`q_{t+h\mid t}(y\mid z)=\mathbf{1}\{y=z\}+hQ_{t}(z,y)+o(h)`$ as
$`h\downarrow 0`$. The reverse rates depend on $`p_{\mathrm{data}}`$,
but conditioning on the clean sample $`Z_{0}`$ makes them computable
from the forward process ([Campbell et al., 2022](#bib.bib5)). For a
change at position $`i`$ from noisy token $`Z_{t}^{i}`$ to another
$`y\neq Z_{t}^{i}`$, the clean-conditioned reverse rates are given by

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
a_{i}(Z_{0},Z_{t},y;t)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}Q_{t}(y,Z_{t}^{i})\frac{q_{t\mid 0}(y\mid Z_{0}^{i})}{q_{t\mid 0}(Z_{t}^{i}\mid Z_{0}^{i})}.
``` |  | (2) |

The true reverse rates are obtained by averaging these clean-conditioned
rates over $`q(Z_{0}\mid Z_{t})`$. Let $`a_{i}^{\theta}(Z_{t},y;t)`$
denote learned reverse rates that depend on the noisy sequence $`Z_{t}`$
and time $`t`$ but not on $`Z_{0}`$. We train them against the
clean-conditioned targets by minimizing the negative of the
continuous-time evidence lower bound (ELBO) ([Campbell et al.,
2022](#bib.bib5); [Casado Noguerales et al., 2026](#bib.bib6)):

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\begin{gathered}-\ELBO(\theta)=\int_{0}^{1}\mathbb{E}_{Z_{0},Z_{t}}[\mathcal{J}_{t}(\theta;Z_{0},Z_{t})]\,dt,\\[2.0pt]
\mathcal{J}_{t}(\theta;Z_{0},Z_{t})=\sum_{i=1}^{L}\sum_{y\neq Z_{t}^{i}}\Phi(a_{i},a_{i}^{\theta}),\qquad\Phi(a,b)=a\log\frac{a}{b}-a+b.\end{gathered}
``` |  | (3) |

This upper-bounds the expected negative log-likelihood. More sharply,
its excess above the data-entropy floor is exactly the path-space KL
between the exact reverse process and the learned reverse
process ([Casado Noguerales et al., 2026](#bib.bib6)). In practice, the
jump rates can become singular near $`t=0`$ or $`t=1`$, so we train on
an interior window $`0<t_{1}<t_{2}<1`$. The corresponding finite-window
objective includes reconstruction and terminal-prior boundary terms,
given in
App. [C.1](#A3.SS1 "C.1 Finite-window negative ELBO and boundary terms ‣ Appendix C Training objectives and time sampling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks").

#### Training.

We parameterize the model reverse rates through a network that takes
$`(Z_{t},t)`$ as input and outputs, at each position $`i`$, a strictly
positive distribution $`\mu_{i}^{\theta}(c\mid Z_{t};t)`$ over clean
tokens $`c\in[V]`$. This induces a noisy-state distribution
$`m_{i}^{\theta}`$, which determines the model reverse rates for
$`y\neq Z_{t}^{i}`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
a_{i}^{\theta}(Z_{t},y;t)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}Q_{t}(y,Z_{t}^{i})\frac{m_{i}^{\theta}(y\mid Z_{t};t)}{m_{i}^{\theta}(Z_{t}^{i}\mid Z_{t};t)},\qquad m_{i}^{\theta}(y\mid Z_{t};t)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}\sum_{c=1}^{V}\mu_{i}^{\theta}(c\mid Z_{t};t)\,q_{t\mid 0}(y\mid c).
``` |  | (4) |

Thus one $`V`$-way network output determines all allowed reverse moves
at a position. Reweighting $`\mu_{i}^{\theta}`$ by the kernel
$`q_{t\mid 0}(Z_{t}^{i}\mid c)`$ gives a new distribution which we
denote by

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\pi_{i}^{\theta}(c\mid Z_{t};t)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}\frac{\mu_{i}^{\theta}(c\mid Z_{t};t)\,q_{t\mid 0}(Z_{t}^{i}\mid c)}{m_{i}^{\theta}(Z_{t}^{i}\mid Z_{t};t)}.
``` |  | (5) |

In terms of this distribution, the model rate
$`a_{i}^{\theta}(Z_{t},y;t)`$
from ([4](#S2.E4 "In Training. ‣ 2 Discrete diffusion modeling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks"))
becomes an average of the clean-conditioned rate
$`a_{i}(Z_{0},Z_{t},y;t)`$
from ([2](#S2.E2 "In 2 Discrete diffusion modeling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")),
where tokens with $`\pi_{i}^{\theta}(c\mid Z_{t};t)=0`$ contribute zero:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
a_{i}^{\theta}(Z_{t},y;t)=Q_{t}(y,Z_{t}^{i})\sum_{c=1}^{V}\pi_{i}^{\theta}(c\mid Z_{t};t)\,\frac{q_{t\mid 0}(y\mid c)}{q_{t\mid 0}(Z_{t}^{i}\mid c)}=\mathbb{E}_{Z_{0}^{i}\sim\pi_{i}^{\theta}(\cdot\mid Z_{t};t)}\big[a_{i}(Z_{0},Z_{t},y;t)\big].
``` |  | (6) |

Training then minimizes an empirical estimate of the path integral
in ([3](#S2.E3 "In 2 Discrete diffusion modeling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks"))
by sampling $`(t,Z_{0},Z_{t})`$.

#### Remark 2.1.

This is the *cavity parameterization* ([Casado Noguerales et al.,
2026](#bib.bib6)). Since the true reverse rates take the averaged
form ([6](#S2.E6 "In Training. ‣ 2 Discrete diffusion modeling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks"))
with the posterior $`q(Z_{0}^{i}\mid Z_{t})`$ in place of
$`\pi_{i}^{\theta}`$, the model rates equal the true rates, and thus
minimize the negative ELBO, when
$`\pi_{i}^{\theta}(c\mid Z_{t};t)=q(Z_{0}^{i}=c\mid Z_{t})`$. This is
attained by setting
$`\mu_{i}^{\theta}(c\mid Z_{t};t)=q(Z_{0}^{i}=c\mid Z_{t}^{-i})`$, the
distribution of the clean token given the rest of the sequence
$`Z_{t}^{-i}`$ (that is, $`Z_{t}`$ excluding $`Z_{t}^{i}`$), even though
the network is evaluated on the full sequence $`Z_{t}`$. We call
$`\pi_{i}^{\theta}`$ the *denoiser* and $`\mu_{i}^{\theta}`$ the
*cavity* predictions or distributions.

## 3 Binary discrete diffusion

In binary diffusion, the noisy state at each position is a *set of
candidate tokens*. We represent a clean token $`c\in[V]`$ by the
singleton $`\{c\}`$, and corruption changes this set by adding or
removing candidates, so that an intermediate state can retain several
alternatives at a single position. Representing each set by its binary
membership vector identifies the noisy state $`Z_{t}^{i}`$ with a vertex
of the binary cube $`\{0,1\}^{V}`$, and we use the same symbol for a
noisy set $`z`$ and its membership vector, including for a clean
singleton $`\{c\}`$ and its one-hot vector. We consider two corruption
processes on this space: binary symmetric diffusion, under which
candidates can be both removed and restored, and binary absorbing
diffusion, which only adds candidates. We focus primarily on the
symmetric process and treat the absorbing process as a simpler monotone
counterpart.

Although the bits evolve independently when conditioned on the clean
sequence $`Z_{0}`$, the true and learned reverse dynamics are generally
correlated across positions and depend on the full noisy sequence.
Crucially, though, the network still produces only the usual $`V`$-way
distribution $`\mu_{i}^{\theta}(c\mid Z_{t};t)`$ over clean tokens at
each position, and the construction of
Section [2](#S2 "2 Discrete diffusion modeling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")
converts this single prediction into all allowed reverse rates on the
binary cube. This is what makes candidate-set diffusion tractable, as we
explain in more detail in
Section [3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Efficient computation and embedding with candidate sets ‣ 3 Binary discrete diffusion ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks").

### 3.1 Binary symmetric diffusion

In binary symmetric diffusion, each membership bit retains its clean
value with probability $`1-t`$ and is otherwise resampled uniformly from
$`\{0,1\}`$. A resampled bit keeps its value half of the time, so a bit
differs from its clean value with probability $`t/2`$, and given
$`Z_{0}`$ the forward process factorizes over positions and bits with
the one-position kernel

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
q_{t\mid 0}^{\mathrm{sym}}(z\mid c)=\Big(1-\frac{t}{2}\Big)^{V-d_{H}(z,c)}\Big(\frac{t}{2}\Big)^{d_{H}(z,c)},
``` |  | (7) |

where $`d_{H}`$ is the Hamming distance. A state at time $`t`$ thus
contains the clean token $`c`$ with probability $`1-t/2`$ and every
other token independently with probability $`t/2`$, so it holds
$`(V-1)t/2`$ false candidates on average, and it approaches independent
fair bits, a uniformly random subset of the vocabulary, as
$`t\uparrow 1`$. More generally, between times $`0\leq s<t<1`$ each bit
is resampled with probability $`(t-s)/(1-s)`$, which gives the
transition kernel

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
q_{t\mid s}^{\mathrm{sym}}(y\mid z)=(1-\varepsilon_{s,t})^{V-d_{H}(y,z)}\,\varepsilon_{s,t}^{d_{H}(y,z)},\qquad\varepsilon_{s,t}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}\frac{t-s}{2(1-s)}.
``` |  | (8) |

#### Forward rates.

Each bit is resampled at rate $`1/(1-t)`$ and changes its value half of
the time, so
differentiating ([8](#S3.E8 "In 3.1 Binary symmetric diffusion ‣ 3 Binary discrete diffusion ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks"))
gives the flip rate

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
Q_{t}^{\mathrm{sym}}\big(z,z^{(u)}\big)=r_{t}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}\frac{1}{2(1-t)},
``` |  | (9) |

where $`z^{(u)}`$ is the state $`z`$ with a single bit $`u`$ flipped,
and every other jump has rate zero. The forward process thus moves along
the edges of the binary cube: from $`z`$, it can only reach the $`V`$
Hamming neighbors $`z^{(1)},\ldots,z^{(V)}`$ of $`z`$ in
$`\{0,1\}^{V}`$.

#### Clean-conditioned reverse rates.

The reverse process traverses the same edges, so each move flips one
bit. We write $`a_{i,u}^{\mathrm{sym}}`$ for the rate of flipping bit
$`u`$ of $`Z_{t}^{i}`$. Since the forward
kernel ([7](#S3.E7 "In 3.1 Binary symmetric diffusion ‣ 3 Binary discrete diffusion ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks"))
factorizes over bits, all unchanged-bit factors cancel in the kernel
ratio
in ([2](#S2.E2 "In 2 Discrete diffusion modeling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")).
The remaining ratio is $`\rho_{t}=(1-t/2)/(t/2)=(2-t)/t`$ when the flip
repairs a mismatch with the clean bit $`(Z_{0}^{i})_{u}`$, and
$`\rho_{t}^{-1}`$ when it creates one. With the forward rate $`r_{t}`$
introduced above, the clean-conditioned rate is therefore

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
a_{i,u}^{\mathrm{sym}}(Z_{0},Z_{t};t)=r_{t}\big[\rho_{t}\,\mathbf{1}\{(Z_{t}^{i})_{u}\neq(Z_{0}^{i})_{u}\}+\rho_{t}^{-1}\,\mathbf{1}\{(Z_{t}^{i})_{u}=(Z_{0}^{i})_{u}\}\big].
``` |  | (10) |

A repairing flip is therefore favored over a corrupting flip by a factor
$`\rho_{t}^{2}`$. This preference strengthens as $`t\downarrow 0`$ and
vanishes as $`t\uparrow 1`$, while both directions remain possible for
$`0<t<1`$.

#### Model reverse rates.

Averaging over the denoiser as
in ([6](#S2.E6 "In Training. ‣ 2 Discrete diffusion modeling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks"))
replaces each indicator
in ([10](#S3.E10 "In Clean-conditioned reverse rates. ‣ 3.1 Binary symmetric diffusion ‣ 3 Binary discrete diffusion ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks"))
by its probability, so that, with $`\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\theta}`$ the
probability under $`Z_{0}^{i}\sim\pi_{i}^{\theta}(\cdot\mid Z_{t};t)`$,
the model reverse rates are

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
a_{i,u}^{\theta,\mathrm{sym}}(Z_{t};t)=r_{t}\big[\rho_{t}\,\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\theta}\{(Z_{t}^{i})_{u}\neq(Z_{0}^{i})_{u}\}+\rho_{t}^{-1}\,\mathbb{P}_{i}^{\theta}\{(Z_{t}^{i})_{u}=(Z_{0}^{i})_{u}\}\big].
``` |  | (11) |

The bit of an active candidate $`u`$ is wrong unless $`u`$ is the clean
token, and the bit of an inactive token is wrong only if it is the clean
token, so removing and restoring a candidate have model reverse rates

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
a_{i,u}^{\theta,\mathrm{sym}}(Z_{t};t)=\begin{cases}r_{t}\big[\rho_{t}\,(1-\pi_{i}^{\theta}(u\mid Z_{t};t))+\rho_{t}^{-1}\,\pi_{i}^{\theta}(u\mid Z_{t};t)\big],&u\in Z_{t}^{i},\\
r_{t}\big[\rho_{t}\,\pi_{i}^{\theta}(u\mid Z_{t};t)+\rho_{t}^{-1}\,(1-\pi_{i}^{\theta}(u\mid Z_{t};t))\big],&u\notin Z_{t}^{i},\end{cases}
``` |  | (12) |

where the denoiser $`\pi_{i}^{\theta}(\cdot\mid Z_{t};t)`$ is the cavity
$`\mu_{i}^{\theta}(\cdot\mid Z_{t};t)`$ multiplied by $`\rho_{t}^{2}`$
on the active candidates of $`Z_{t}^{i}`$ and renormalized.

### 3.2 Binary absorbing diffusion

Binary absorbing diffusion only adds candidates: between times
$`0\leq s<t<1`$, each inactive bit activates independently with
probability $`(t-s)/(1-s)`$, and active bits never flip. Its kernel and
forward rates are therefore

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
q_{t\mid s}^{\mathrm{abs}}(y\mid z)=\mathbf{1}\{z\subseteq y\}\Big(\frac{1-t}{1-s}\Big)^{V-|y|}\Big(\frac{t-s}{1-s}\Big)^{|y|-|z|},\qquad Q_{t}^{\mathrm{abs}}\big(z,z^{(u)}\big)=\frac{\mathbf{1}\{u\notin z\}}{1-t},
``` |  | (13) |

and every other jump has rate zero. In particular,
$`q_{t\mid 0}^{\mathrm{abs}}(z\mid c)=\mathbf{1}\{c\in z\}(1-t)^{V-|z|}t^{|z|-1}`$:
the clean token $`c`$ always remains a candidate and every other token
becomes one independently with probability $`t`$, so the state holds
$`(V-1)t`$ false candidates on average and approaches the full
vocabulary as $`t\uparrow 1`$.

Since the forward process only adds candidates, the reverse process only
removes them. Removing a false candidate gives the kernel ratio
$`(1-t)/t`$ in the clean-conditioned
rate ([2](#S2.E2 "In 2 Discrete diffusion modeling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")),
while the clean token cannot be removed, so this rate and its
average ([6](#S2.E6 "In Training. ‣ 2 Discrete diffusion modeling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks"))
over the denoiser $`\pi_{i}^{\theta}`$ are

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
a_{i,u}^{\mathrm{abs}}(Z_{0},Z_{t};t)=\frac{\mathbf{1}\{u\in Z_{t}^{i}\setminus Z_{0}^{i}\}}{t},\qquad a_{i,u}^{\theta,\mathrm{abs}}(Z_{t};t)=\frac{\mathbf{1}\{u\in Z_{t}^{i}\}}{t}\big(1-\pi_{i}^{\theta}(u\mid Z_{t};t)\big),
``` |  | (14) |

where $`\pi_{i}^{\theta}(\cdot\mid Z_{t};t)`$ is the renormalized
restriction of $`\mu_{i}^{\theta}(\cdot\mid Z_{t};t)`$ to the active
candidates of $`Z_{t}^{i}`$.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### 3.3 Efficient computation and embedding with candidate sets

Candidate-set diffusion has $`2^{V}`$ possible states per position,
which a priori require work exponential in $`V`$ for computing the model
rates and the ELBO loss. However, parameterizing in terms of a
clean-data distribution allows us to work in $`O(V)`$ per position,
without enumerating the exponentially many possible candidate sets. For
the rates, every reverse jump flips a single bit, so the reverse process
can only move from a state $`z`$ to its $`V`$ Hamming neighbors
$`z^{(u)}`$. After one network evaluation, the denoiser
$`\pi_{i}^{\theta}`$ of a position follows from $`\mu_{i}^{\theta}`$ by
reweighting and normalization in $`O(V)`$ time, and each of the $`V`$
flip rates
$`a_{i,u}^{\theta}`$, ([12](#S3.E12 "In Model reverse rates. ‣ 3.1 Binary symmetric diffusion ‣ 3 Binary discrete diffusion ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks"))
or ([14](#S3.E14 "In 3.2 Binary absorbing diffusion ‣ 3 Binary discrete diffusion ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")),
then takes constant work. For the same reason, the path loss
in ([3](#S2.E3 "In 2 Discrete diffusion modeling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks"))
sums only over these $`V`$ moves per position $`i`$,
$`\mathcal{J}_{t}=\smash[t]{\sum_{i}\sum_{u=1}^{V}\Phi(a_{i,u},a_{i,u}^{\theta})}`$.
App. [B](#A2 "Appendix B Mathematical details of binary diffusion ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")
derives all rates and losses in full detail.

Similarly, to avoid materializing an embedding table over the $`2^{V}`$
states, we embed a candidate set by applying the input embedding matrix
$`E\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times d}`$, whose row $`E_{c}`$ embeds clean token
$`c\in[V]`$, to its $`\ell_{2}`$-normalized membership vector,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
e(z)=E^{\top}\frac{z}{\|z\|_{2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{|z|}}\sum_{c\in z}E_{c},\qquad e(\emptyset)=0.
``` |  | (15) |

This costs $`O(V)`$ and reduces to the ordinary token embedding
$`E_{c}`$ for a singleton $`\{c\}`$. Apart from this input layer, we
therefore use the same architecture as for the masked and uniform
baselines.

### 3.4 Information loss and the time schedule

Figure 2: Fraction of the information retained for independent,
uniformly distributed tokens with $`V=1024`$, against the
reparameterized time $`\xi`$ of the linear (left) and logarithmic
(right) schedules.

In binary diffusion, the first false candidate doubles the number of
candidates for the clean token, whereas each later one enlarges an
already large set. Since false candidates appear at a rate proportional
to $`V`$, the binary kernels thus erase the clean token much faster than
masked and uniform diffusion at large vocabularies.

We quantify the retained information by the mutual information
$`I(Z_{0}^{i};Z_{t}^{i})=H(Z_{0}^{i})-H(Z_{0}^{i}\mid Z_{t}^{i})`$, the
reduction in uncertainty about the clean token from observing its noisy
state, where $`H`$ denotes Shannon entropy. Since
$`I(Z_{0}^{i};Z_{t}^{i})`$ is intractable in general, we do so on a
reference distribution of independent, uniformly distributed tokens
(App. [C.4](#A3.SS4 "C.4 Information retained under each kernel ‣ Appendix C Training objectives and time sampling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")).
Masked and uniform diffusion then lose information roughly linearly in
$`t`$, whereas the binary kernels lose it roughly logarithmically, so
that a uniform sample of $`t`$ places most training times where little
information is left
(Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3.4 Information loss and the time schedule ‣ 3 Binary discrete diffusion ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks"),
left).

This reference calculation motivates a change of
clock ([Casado Noguerales et al., 2026](#bib.bib6)): a time
reparameterization $`\xi\mapsto t`$, with $`\xi`$ drawn uniformly from
$`[0,1]`$, to control how fast information is destroyed. Reweighting the
path integrand $`\mathcal{J}_{t}`$ by $`dt/d\xi`$ then leaves the ELBO
objective ([3](#S2.E3 "In 2 Discrete diffusion modeling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks"))
unchanged, so that only the allocation of training times changes. With a
logarithmic map instead of the linear one,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
t_{\mathrm{lin}}(\xi)=t_{1}+(t_{2}-t_{1})\,\xi,\qquad t_{\log}(\xi)=t_{1}\Big(\frac{t_{2}}{t_{1}}\Big)^{\xi},
``` |  | (16) |

the binary kernels lose their information approximately linearly in
$`\xi`$
(Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3.4 Information loss and the time schedule ‣ 3 Binary discrete diffusion ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks"),
right). We also give $`\xi`$ to the network as its time input rather
than $`t`$. For $`V\geq 1024`$, the logarithmic schedule substantially
improved optimization. For the smaller vocabularies ($`V\leq 9`$) of our
logic tasks, this choice made no difference and all kernels trained
successfully with the linear schedule. We further refine all time
schedules with an adaptive time sampler (see
Apps. [C.3](#A3.SS3 "C.3 Time schedules ‣ Appendix C Training objectives and time sampling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")
and [C.5](#A3.SS5 "C.5 Adaptive gradient-RMS importance sampling ‣ Appendix C Training objectives and time sampling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")
for the details).

## 4 Sampling

Generation runs the learned reverse process on a grid
$`t_{2}=\tau_{N}>\cdots>\tau_{0}=t_{1}`$, starting from a prior
distribution $`p_{t_{2}}`$ and ending with a final decoding step via the
denoiser $`\pi_{i}^{\theta}(\cdot\mid Z_{t_{1}};t_{1})`$. As priors we
take the limiting forward distributions, a uniformly random subset of
the vocabulary for binary symmetric and the full vocabulary, given by
the all-ones vector $`\mathds{1}_{V}`$, for binary absorbing:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
p_{t_{2}}^{\mathrm{sym}}(z)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}2^{-V},\qquad p_{t_{2}}^{\mathrm{abs}}(z)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}\mathbf{1}\{z=\mathds{1}_{V}\}.
``` |  | (17) |

#### Ancestral sampling.

Ancestral sampling from a time $`t`$ to the next time $`s<t`$ of the
grid follows the reverse process learned through the ELBO, so that as
$`t\downarrow s`$, its jump rates approach the model
rates ([6](#S2.E6 "In Training. ‣ 2 Discrete diffusion modeling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")).
At each step, it updates the positions independently given $`Z_{t}`$ by
averaging the *bridge* $`q_{s\mid t,0}(y\mid z,c)`$, the distribution of
$`Z_{s}^{i}=y`$ given $`Z_{t}^{i}=z`$ and $`Z_{0}^{i}=c`$, over the
denoiser:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
p_{s\mid t,i}^{\theta}(y\mid Z_{t})=\sum_{c=1}^{V}\pi_{i}^{\theta}(c\mid Z_{t};t)\,q_{s\mid t,0}(y\mid Z_{t}^{i},c).
``` |  | (18) |

As in
Section [3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Efficient computation and embedding with candidate sets ‣ 3 Binary discrete diffusion ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks"),
we avoid enumerating the $`2^{V}`$ states: given the clean token, the
forward process corrupts the bits independently, so the bridge factors
over bits,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
q_{s\mid t,0}(y\mid z,c)=\prod_{u=1}^{V}q_{s\mid t,0}\big(y_{u}\mid z_{u},\mathbf{1}\{u=c\}\big).
``` |  | (19) |

Thus, each bit’s factor accounts for every sequence of jumps between
$`s`$ and $`t`$, and a step can change many bits without simulating
jumps or Poisson counts. The
mixture ([18](#S4.E18 "In Ancestral sampling. ‣ 4 Sampling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks"))
does not factor over bits, but we can still sample it exactly at a cost
of $`O(V)`$ per position without enumerating the $`2^{V}`$ possible
states: we draw a clean proposal
$`\mathchoice{\widehat{Z}_{0}^{i}}{\smash[t]{\widehat{Z}_{0}^{i}}\vphantom{Z_{0}^{i}}}{\widehat{Z}_{0}^{i}}{\widehat{Z}_{0}^{i}}{}\sim\pi_{i}^{\theta}(\cdot\mid Z_{t};t)`$
and then sample each bit independently
from ([19](#S4.E19 "In Ancestral sampling. ‣ 4 Sampling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks"))
with
$`c=\mathchoice{\widehat{Z}_{0}^{i}}{\smash[t]{\widehat{Z}_{0}^{i}}\vphantom{Z_{0}^{i}}}{\widehat{Z}_{0}^{i}}{\widehat{Z}_{0}^{i}}{}`$
(App. [B.3](#A2.SS3 "B.3 Binary ancestral bridges ‣ Appendix B Mathematical details of binary diffusion ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")).
Under the symmetric bridge, each bit favors its current value for $`s`$
close to $`t`$ and the proposal’s value as $`s\downarrow 0`$, so removed
candidates can return, whereas the absorbing bridge always retains the
clean proposal and independently retains each other active candidate
with probability $`s/t`$.

#### Revision by re-corruption.

Ancestral sampling conditions each step on the current state $`Z_{t}`$,
which biases it toward what earlier steps have decided, including their
mistakes. *Re-corrupt* sampling instead forgets the current state: it
averages the kernel $`q_{s\mid 0}`$ rather than the bridge
$`q_{s\mid t,0}`$,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
p_{s\mid t,i}^{\theta,\mathrm{re\text{-}corr}}(y\mid Z_{t})=\sum_{c=1}^{V}\pi_{i}^{\theta}(c\mid Z_{t};t)\,q_{s\mid 0}(y\mid c),
``` |  | (20) |

which we again sample in two steps by drawing a clean proposal
$`\mathchoice{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}{\smash[t]{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}\vphantom{Z_{0}^{i}}}{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}{}\sim\pi_{i}^{\theta}(\cdot\mid Z_{t};t)`$
and then corrupting it afresh to noise level $`s`$. With an exact
denoiser, both updates preserve the per-position forward marginals, but
re-corruption makes every position revisable at every step.
Interestingly, re-corruption alone markedly improves solve rates on
logic tasks
(Table [10](#A6.T10 "Table 10 ‣ F.4 Sampler tuning procedure ‣ Appendix F Experimental details ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks"),
App. [F.4](#A6.SS4 "F.4 Sampler tuning procedure ‣ Appendix F Experimental details ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")).

#### Confidence-guided $`\Psi`$-sampler.

As in the $`\Psi`$-sampler of [Deschenaux et al. (2026)](#bib.bib12), we
mix the ancestral and re-corrupt updates, but independently at each
position $`i`$ with weight $`\kappa_{i}`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathchoice{\widehat{Z}_{0}^{i}}{\smash[t]{\widehat{Z}_{0}^{i}}\vphantom{Z_{0}^{i}}}{\widehat{Z}_{0}^{i}}{\widehat{Z}_{0}^{i}}{},\mathchoice{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}{\smash[t]{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}\vphantom{Z_{0}^{i}}}{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}{}\sim\pi_{i}^{\theta}(\cdot\mid Z_{t};t),\qquad Z_{s}^{i}\sim(1-\kappa_{i})\,q_{s\mid t,0}(\cdot\mid Z_{t}^{i},\mathchoice{\widehat{Z}_{0}^{i}}{\smash[t]{\widehat{Z}_{0}^{i}}\vphantom{Z_{0}^{i}}}{\widehat{Z}_{0}^{i}}{\widehat{Z}_{0}^{i}}{})+\kappa_{i}\,q_{s\mid 0}(\cdot\mid\mathchoice{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}{\smash[t]{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}\vphantom{Z_{0}^{i}}}{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}{}),
``` |  | (21) |

where we draw the two proposals independently and where $`\kappa_{i}`$
may depend on the re-corrupted proposal
$`\mathchoice{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}{\smash[t]{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}\vphantom{Z_{0}^{i}}}{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}{}`$.
A constant $`\kappa_{i}=\eta`$ interpolates from ancestral sampling at
$`\eta=0`$ to re-corrupt sampling at $`\eta=1`$ and preserves the
per-position marginals, since both updates do. For masked diffusion,
this mixture is the remasking sampler ReMDM ([Wang et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib58)). We extend it with two confidence mechanisms,
position confidence with strengths $`\gamma`$ and $`\lambda`$ and
candidate confidence with strength $`\beta`$, which recover the plain
$`\Psi`$-sampler at zero
(Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ Confidence-guided Ψ-sampler. ‣ 4 Sampling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks");
full details specified in
App. [D](#A4 "Appendix D Confidence-guided Ψ-sampler ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")).

- •
  Position confidence: where to reconsider. Following ReMDM-conf, we use
  the model’s confidence in its clean proposal
  $`\mathchoice{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}{\smash[t]{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}\vphantom{Z_{0}^{i}}}{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}{}`$,
  read from the cavity or the denoiser, to concentrate revision on
  uncertain positions. We let $`\kappa_{i}`$ decrease with confidence at
  strength $`\gamma`$, keeping its mean equal to $`\eta`$ across
  positions. We also tilt the noise level $`s_{i}`$ to which
  re-corrupted positions return with the same confidence at strength
  $`\lambda`$, keeping the mean noise level at $`s`$.
- •
  Candidate confidence: which candidates to reconsider. Plain
  re-corruption reopens alternative candidates uniformly at random, as
  the forward kernel does. For binary diffusion, we instead reopen
  candidate $`u`$ with probability proportional to $`p_{i,u}^{\beta}`$,
  keeping the expected number of reopened candidates fixed, where
  $`p_{i,u}`$ is the denoiser probability of $`u`$ when it was last in
  the candidate set. Uniform diffusion analogously draws the new token
  $`u\neq\mathchoice{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}{\smash[t]{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}\vphantom{Z_{0}^{i}}}{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}{}`$
  in proportion to $`\pi_{i}^{\theta}(u\mid Z_{t};t)^{\beta}`$, while
  masked diffusion has no candidate to reopen. Plausible candidates are
  thus preferentially restored.

1: Cavity model, kernel, grid $`t_{2}=\tau_{N}>\cdots>\tau_{0}=t_{1}`$,
re-corrupt fraction $`\eta`$, strengths $`\gamma,\lambda,\beta`$,
temperature $`T`$

2: Draw $`Z_{t_{2}}^{i}\sim p_{t_{2}}`$ and set $`p_{i,u}=1/V`$ for all
$`i,u`$.

3: for $`j=N,\ldots,1`$ do

4:   Set $`t=\tau_{j}`$, $`s=\tau_{j-1}`$, evaluate
$`\mu_{i}^{\theta}(\cdot\mid Z_{t};t)`$, compute $`\pi_{i}^{\theta}`$
by ([5](#S2.E5 "In Training. ‣ 2 Discrete diffusion modeling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")),
and record $`p_{i,u}={\pi_{i}^{\theta}(u\mid Z_{t};t)}`$ for
$`u\in Z_{t}^{i}`$ (every $`u`$ for uniform diffusion).

5:   Draw a proposal
$`\mathchoice{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}{\smash[t]{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}\vphantom{Z_{0}^{i}}}{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}{}\propto\pi_{i}^{\theta}(\cdot\mid Z_{t};t)^{1/T}`$
and read its confidence $`\mathrm{conf}_{i}`$ from $`\mu_{i}^{\theta}`$
or $`\pi_{i}^{\theta}`$.

6:   Set $`\kappa_{i}\propto\exp(-\gamma\,\mathrm{conf}_{i})`$ and
$`s_{i}\propto\exp(-\lambda\,\mathrm{conf}_{i})`$, capped at one, with
means $`\eta`$ and $`s`$ over positions (using
equations ([65](#A4.E65 "In Position confidence 𝛾. ‣ Appendix D Confidence-guided Ψ-sampler ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks"))
and ([66](#A4.E66 "In Ordering tilt 𝜆. ‣ Appendix D Confidence-guided Ψ-sampler ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")),
App. [D](#A4 "Appendix D Confidence-guided Ψ-sampler ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")).

7:   With probability $`\kappa_{i}`$, re-corrupt
$`\mathchoice{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}{\smash[t]{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}\vphantom{Z_{0}^{i}}}{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}{}`$
to $`s_{i}`$, reopening candidates $`u`$ with
probability $`\propto p_{i,u}^{\beta}`$, and otherwise draw
$`Z_{s}^{i}`$ from the ancestral
update ([18](#S4.E18 "In Ancestral sampling. ‣ 4 Sampling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks"))
with its own proposal
$`\mathchoice{\widehat{Z}_{0}^{i}}{\smash[t]{\widehat{Z}_{0}^{i}}\vphantom{Z_{0}^{i}}}{\widehat{Z}_{0}^{i}}{\widehat{Z}_{0}^{i}}{}`$.

8: end for

9: Sample each position
$`\propto\pi_{i}^{\theta}(\cdot\mid Z_{t_{1}};t_{1})^{1/T}`$, only the
masked ones for masked diffusion.

Algorithm 1 Confidence-guided $`\Psi`$-sampler (full details specified
in
App. [D](#A4 "Appendix D Confidence-guided Ψ-sampler ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")).

## 5 Experiments

We focus on solve rate and sample quality and report negative ELBOs only
for completeness: the negative ELBO measures the path-space KL to the
exact reverse process ([Casado Noguerales et al., 2026](#bib.bib6)), but
it need not track the quality of the final samples, especially under
non-ancestral samplers, as uniform versus masked diffusion
shows ([Schiff et al., 2025](#bib.bib45); [Sahoo et al.,
2025](#bib.bib41)).

### 5.1 Logic and planning tasks

We evaluate on Sudoku-Extreme ([Wang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib57)),
Boxoban ([Guez et al., 2018](#bib.bib21); [Garriga-Alonso et al.,
2024](#bib.bib17)), and four-coloring of random graphs, using matched
43M-parameter diffusion transformers and five training seeds per kernel
and task. Besides the full test sets, we report hard subsets to
de-saturate the benchmarks: low-clue Sudoku, long-solution Boxoban, and
graphs ten times the training size. A sample counts as solved only if it
satisfies every constraint, with one attempt per instance and no
verifier. For the full and hard settings separately, we select each
kernel’s sampler on validation at a reference budget of 256 network
evaluations (NFE) for Sudoku and Boxoban and 64 for graph coloring, with
the same tuning budget for every kernel and candidate confidence for all
but masked diffusion. Parentheses below are standard errors over the
five training seeds. Full experimental details are given in
App. [F](#A6 "Appendix F Experimental details ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks"),
and the test negative ELBOs in
Table [6](#A6.T6 "Table 6 ‣ F.2 Learning-rate and checkpoint selection ‣ Appendix F Experimental details ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks").

|  | Sudoku |  | Boxoban |  | Graph coloring |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Kernel | All | Hard | All | Hard | All | Hard |
| Binary symmetric | 96.27 (0.21) | 92.66 (0.39) | 94.29 (0.30) | 84.65 (0.56) | 99.35 (0.00) | 64.13 (1.10) |
| Uniform | 95.47 (0.21) | 89.81 (0.47) | 92.38 (0.64) | 78.73 (1.20) | 99.01 (0.02) | 61.41 (0.34) |
| Binary absorbing | 91.24 (0.11) | 81.08 (0.26) | 87.30 (0.81) | 69.13 (1.66) | 98.83 (0.02) | 54.77 (0.39) |
| Masked | 87.96 (0.16) | 76.12 (0.10) | 91.26 (0.31) | 75.47 (0.69) | 97.44 (0.04) | 4.85 (0.33) |

reports the solve rates at the reference NFE, while

shows their dependence on inference budget and training progress. Binary

ablates the sampling components, while

in

### 5.2 Text

We compare the four kernels using unconditional generation on three
corpora of increasing sequence length $`L`$: Text8 ([Mahoney,
2011](#bib.bib32)) at $`L=256`$, TinyStories ([Eldan & Li,
2023](#bib.bib13)) at $`L=512`$, and OpenWebText ([Gokaslan & Cohen,
2019](#bib.bib18)) at $`L=1024`$
(App. [F.6](#A6.SS6 "F.6 Language modeling ‣ Appendix F Experimental details ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")).
We train every model on 131B tokens, on Text8 at the character level
with $`V=27`$ and on TinyStories and OpenWebText with byte-pair-encoding
tokenizers of $`V=1024`$, using as training objective the path term of
the negative
ELBO ([3](#S2.E3 "In 2 Discrete diffusion modeling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks"))
(except for masked and binary absorbing diffusion on Text8, see
App. [C.2](#A3.SS2 "C.2 Training objectives ‣ Appendix C Training objectives and time sampling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")).
We report MAUVE ([Pillutla et al., 2021](#bib.bib36)) against GPT-2
token unigram entropy, with GPT-2 Large ([Radford et al.,
2019](#bib.bib38)) supplying the features. MAUVE compares the
distribution of generated samples with held-out text, and we use it as
the primary metric given known failure modes of generative perplexity
(GenPPL) ([Franca & Tong, 2026](#bib.bib16); [Zheng et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib65)), which we report with the negative ELBOs in
App. [F.6](#A6.SS6 "F.6 Language modeling ‣ Appendix F Experimental details ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks").

Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 5.2 Text ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")
gives the test MAUVE of each kernel at the sampler setting selected on
validation
(App. [F.4](#A6.SS4 "F.4 Sampler tuning procedure ‣ Appendix F Experimental details ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")),
while
Figure [4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 5.2 Text ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")
traces quality against diversity using sampling settings selected on
validation at representative entropies and evaluated on the test split.
No kernel leads on all three corpora: binary symmetric diffusion reaches
the best MAUVE on Text8, uniform diffusion on TinyStories, and masked
diffusion on OpenWebText, each by a small margin. The kernels peak at
slightly different entropies, so
Table [12](#A6.T12 "Table 12 ‣ OpenWebText. ‣ F.6 Language modeling ‣ Appendix F Experimental details ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")
in
App. [F.6](#A6.SS6 "F.6 Language modeling ‣ Appendix F Experimental details ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")
also compares them at one common entropy per corpus, where binary
symmetric diffusion reaches the best MAUVE on both Text8 and
TinyStories.

## 6 Related work

Discrete diffusion was first formulated on a discrete time grid,
modeling the reverse transitions directly ([Hoogeboom et al.,
2021](#bib.bib23); [Austin et al., 2021](#bib.bib1)), and its
continuous-time formulation instead learns to reverse a categorical jump
process ([Campbell et al., 2022](#bib.bib5); [Sun et al.,
2023](#bib.bib52)). Since then, methods have differed mainly in how they
parameterize the reverse rates ([Lou et al., 2024](#bib.bib31); [Ou
et al., 2025](#bib.bib33)) and in which paths the forward process
allows ([von Rütte et al., 2025](#bib.bib56); [Shaul et al.,
2025](#bib.bib47)). Closer to our setting, simplex-valued methods
represent categorical uncertainty in a continuous state ([Floto et al.,
2023](#bib.bib15); [Avdeyev et al., 2023](#bib.bib2)), while partial and
semantic masking keep residual information about the clean token ([Chao
et al., 2025](#bib.bib8); [Zhou et al., 2025](#bib.bib66)). Binary
diffusion instead changes the state space: each position follows a jump
process on the binary cube, whose coordinates express candidate
membership. Similar bit-flipping processes have been explored to model
binary data, where the cube is the data space ([Sohl-Dickstein et al.,
2015](#bib.bib49); [Pham et al., 2025](#bib.bib35)). The closest
predecessor is the ShortListing Model, which also grows candidate sets,
in discrete time ([Song et al., 2025](#bib.bib50)). Under the right
noise schedule, its corruption process provides a discrete-time
formulation of binary absorbing diffusion
(App. [E](#A5 "Appendix E Extended related work ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")).
Our main contributions are the non-absorbing symmetric process, which
allows candidates to be both removed and restored during denoising, and
the empirical evaluation on logic and planning tasks.

Discrete diffusion has been applied to Sudoku and other structured
problems before ([Ye et al., 2025](#bib.bib62); [Wewer et al.,
2025](#bib.bib60)), and follow-up work improves solving through adaptive
token order, remasking, explicit planning, or test-time search ([Kim
et al., 2025](#bib.bib27); [Wang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib58); [Liu
et al., 2025](#bib.bib30); [Zhang et al., 2026](#bib.bib63)). Sudoku is
also a standard benchmark for small recurrent reasoners such as HRM and
TRM ([Wang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib57); [Jolicoeur-Martineau,
2025](#bib.bib25)), and Lattice Deduction Transformers likewise maintain
per-variable candidate sets but train deduction on-policy with search
and abstention heuristics ([Davis et al., 2026](#bib.bib11)). All of
these change the sampler, the architecture, or the training signal. Our
experiments are instead designed to isolate the effect of the corruption
kernel and evaluate direct, verifier-free samples from each kernel’s
tuned sampler.

## 7 Conclusion

We have introduced Binary Discrete Diffusion, a family of
continuous-time discrete-diffusion processes whose noisy states are sets
of candidate tokens, represented as binary membership vectors.
Parameterizing the reverse process through clean-token predictions lets
a single $`V`$-way output determine all reverse rates and sampling
updates, avoiding any $`2^{V}`$ enumeration in training and generation.
We also introduced a confidence-guided self-correcting sampler that
chooses which positions and candidates to reopen. Under controlled
architectures, training budgets, and sampler tuning, binary symmetric
diffusion outperforms uniform diffusion, and both outperform masked and
binary absorbing diffusion on logic and planning tasks, with the largest
gains on the hardest instances. Binary diffusion also remains
competitive on language modeling. Our results thus show that candidate
sets can be an effective intermediate representation for iterative
reasoning, and that the corruption process can materially change the
computation learned by the model.

Binary diffusion also opens a broader design space for candidate-set and
bitwise corruption processes. Future kernels could exploit semantic or
task-specific structure to introduce plausible candidates rather than
random ones. The bits could also encode tokens differently, for example
through their binary indices or an error-correcting code, although each
such code defines a different state space whose states are no longer
candidate sets. Richer representations of candidate sets than the
normalized embedding sum used here may also prove useful at larger
scales. Scaling these ideas to larger models and datasets, and to
domains such as code, mathematics, and biological sequence design, is a
natural next step.

### AI use statement

Large language models were used to aid and polish writing (editing and
reviewing the manuscript), for retrieval and discovery (finding and
summarizing related work), and for research ideation and execution
(implementing, running, and analyzing experiments). All AI-assisted work
was reviewed by the authors, who verified every technical claim and
result and take full responsibility for the final content.

### Reproducibility statement

App. [F](#A6 "Appendix F Experimental details ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")
specifies the datasets with their splits and hard subsets, the
architectures and training settings, every evaluation procedure, and the
selection of learning rates, checkpoints, and sampler settings.
App. [C](#A3 "Appendix C Training objectives and time sampling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")
describes the training objectives and time sampling,
Apps. [A](#A1 "Appendix A Masked and uniform diffusion ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")
and [B](#A2 "Appendix B Mathematical details of binary diffusion ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")
derive the rates, losses, and ancestral updates of every kernel, and
App. [D](#A4 "Appendix D Confidence-guided Ψ-sampler ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")
specifies the sampler.
````
