````math
## Appendix contents

## Appendix A Masked and uniform diffusion

We specialize the results of [Campbell et al. (2022)](#bib.bib5)
and [Casado Noguerales et al. (2026)](#bib.bib6) using the notation of
Sections [2](#S2 "2 Discrete diffusion modeling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")–[4](#S4 "4 Sampling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks").
Local noisy states are written $`z,y`$, and the priors are the limiting
distributions from which generation starts. We call the noisy-state
distribution $`m_{i}^{\theta}`$
in ([4](#S2.E4 "In Training. ‣ 2 Discrete diffusion modeling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks"))
the local model mass.

### A.1 Masked diffusion

For the masked kernel
in ([1](#S2.E1 "In 2 Discrete diffusion modeling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")),
the off-diagonal forward rates are ([Casado Noguerales et al.,
2026](#bib.bib6))

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
Q_{t}(z,y)=\frac{\mathbf{1}\{z\in[V],\ y=\mathtt{m}\}}{1-t},\qquad y\neq z.
``` |  | (22) |

For $`0\leq s<t<1`$, the transition kernel is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
q_{t\mid s}(y\mid z)=\frac{1-t}{1-s}\,\mathbf{1}\{y=z\}+\frac{t-s}{1-s}\,\mathbf{1}\{y=\mathtt{m}\}.
``` |  | (23) |

The local model masses and denoiser are

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle m_{i}^{\theta}(y\mid Z_{t};t)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\begin{cases}(1-t)\,\mu_{i}^{\theta}(y\mid Z_{t};t),&y\in[V],\\
t,&y=\mathtt{m},\end{cases}`$ |  | (24) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\pi_{i}^{\theta}(c\mid Z_{t};t)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\mu_{i}^{\theta}(c\mid Z_{t};t),&Z_{t}^{i}=\mathtt{m},\\
\mathbf{1}\{Z_{t}^{i}=c\},&Z_{t}^{i}\in[V].\end{cases}`$ |  |  |

For $`y\in[V]`$ with $`y\neq Z_{t}^{i}`$, the reverse rates are

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
a_{i}(Z_{0},Z_{t},y;t)=\frac{\mathbf{1}\{Z_{t}^{i}=\mathtt{m},\ y=Z_{0}^{i}\}}{t},\qquad a_{i}^{\theta}(Z_{t},y;t)=\frac{\mathbf{1}\{Z_{t}^{i}=\mathtt{m}\}\,\mu_{i}^{\theta}(y\mid Z_{t};t)}{t}.
``` |  | (25) |

All other off-diagonal reverse rates vanish. The path loss reduces to
masked cross-entropy:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{J}_{t}(\theta;Z_{0},Z_{t})=-\frac{1}{t}\sum_{i}\mathbf{1}\{Z_{t}^{i}=\mathtt{m}\}\log\mu_{i}^{\theta}(Z_{0}^{i}\mid Z_{t};t).
``` |  | (26) |

Plugging $`\mu_{i}^{\theta}`$ into the
bridge ([47](#A2.E47 "In B.3 Binary ancestral bridges ‣ Appendix B Mathematical details of binary diffusion ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks"))
gives the ancestral update of [Sahoo et al. (2024)](#bib.bib40): visible
tokens are copied, and a masked position unmasks to $`c`$ with
probability $`(1-s/t)\,\mu_{i}^{\theta}(c\mid Z_{t};t)`$.

### A.2 Uniform diffusion

For the uniform kernel
in ([1](#S2.E1 "In 2 Discrete diffusion modeling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")),
the off-diagonal forward rates are ([Casado Noguerales et al.,
2026](#bib.bib6))

|     |                                             |     |      |
|-----|---------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       Q_{t}(z,y)=\frac{1}{V(1-t)},\qquad y\neq z.
       ```                                          |     | (27) |

For $`0\leq s<t<1`$, the transition kernel is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
q_{t\mid s}(y\mid z)=\frac{1-t}{1-s}\,\mathbf{1}\{y=z\}+\frac{t-s}{V(1-s)}.
``` |  | (28) |

The local model mass and induced denoiser are

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle m_{i}^{\theta}(y\mid Z_{t};t)`$ | $`\displaystyle=(1-t)\,\mu_{i}^{\theta}(y\mid Z_{t};t)+t/V,`$ |  | (29) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\pi_{i}^{\theta}(c\mid Z_{t};t)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{\mu_{i}^{\theta}(c\mid Z_{t};t)\,[(1-t)\,\mathbf{1}\{Z_{t}^{i}=c\}+t/V]}{(1-t)\,\mu_{i}^{\theta}(Z_{t}^{i}\mid Z_{t};t)+t/V}.`$ |  |  |

For $`y\neq Z_{t}^{i}`$, the clean-conditioned and model reverse rates
are

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle a_{i}(Z_{0},Z_{t},y;t)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1}{V(1-t)}\frac{(1-t)\,\mathbf{1}\{y=Z_{0}^{i}\}+t/V}{(1-t)\,\mathbf{1}\{Z_{t}^{i}=Z_{0}^{i}\}+t/V},`$ |  | (30) |
|  | $`\displaystyle a_{i}^{\theta}(Z_{t},y;t)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1}{V(1-t)}\frac{(1-t)\,\mu_{i}^{\theta}(y\mid Z_{t};t)+t/V}{(1-t)\,\mu_{i}^{\theta}(Z_{t}^{i}\mid Z_{t};t)+t/V}.`$ |  |  |

The path loss is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{J}_{t}(\theta;Z_{0},Z_{t})=\frac{1}{V(1-t)}\sum_{i}\sum_{y\neq Z_{t}^{i}}\Phi\left(\frac{q_{t\mid 0}(y\mid Z_{0}^{i})}{q_{t\mid 0}(Z_{t}^{i}\mid Z_{0}^{i})},\frac{m_{i}^{\theta}(y\mid Z_{t};t)}{m_{i}^{\theta}(Z_{t}^{i}\mid Z_{t};t)}\right).
``` |  | (31) |

All masses in these quotients are positive on an interior time interval.

Plugging $`\mu_{i}^{\theta}`$ into the
bridge ([47](#A2.E47 "In B.3 Binary ancestral bridges ‣ Appendix B Mathematical details of binary diffusion ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks"))
gives the ancestral update of [Schiff et al. (2025)](#bib.bib45), which,
unlike the masked update, can change a visible token.

#### Prior term.

Corrupting a uniform clean token leaves its distribution uniform. The
finite-time and limiting priors thus coincide:

|     |                                  |     |      |
|-----|----------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       p_{t_{2}}(y)=1/V,\qquad y\in[V].
       ```                               |     | (32) |

For the product sequence prior,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{E}_{Z_{0}}\operatorname{KL}\big(q_{t_{2}\mid 0}(\cdot\mid Z_{0})\,\|\,p_{t_{2}}\big)=L\left[(1-t_{2}+t_{2}/V)\log\big(V(1-t_{2})+t_{2}\big)+\frac{(V-1)t_{2}}{V}\log t_{2}\right].
``` |  | (33) |

The uniform prior has full support at every finite cutoff.

## Appendix B Mathematical details of binary diffusion

We use the candidate-set notation and the bitwise loss from
Section [3](#S3 "3 Binary discrete diffusion ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks").
The network probability mass of the candidates in a set $`z`$ is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\nu_{i}^{\theta}(z\mid Z_{t};t)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}\sum_{c\in z}\mu_{i}^{\theta}(c\mid Z_{t};t),
``` |  | (34) |

and $`m_{i}^{\theta}`$ denotes the local model mass
of ([4](#S2.E4 "In Training. ‣ 2 Discrete diffusion modeling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")).
Superscripts $`\mathrm{sym}`$ and $`\mathrm{abs}`$ specify the kernel,
and we omit them in derivations where it is fixed. The cavity
$`\mu_{i}^{\theta}`$, the masses $`m_{i}^{\theta}`$, and the denoiser
$`\pi_{i}^{\theta}`$ always refer to that kernel.

### B.1 Binary symmetric diffusion

###### Proposition B.1 (Symmetric kernel and reverse rates).

Let each bit flip at rate $`1/[2(1-t)]`$. For $`0\leq s<t<1`$, the
probability of a bit differing from its value at $`s`$ is

|     |                                       |     |      |
|-----|---------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \varepsilon_{s,t}=\frac{t-s}{2(1-s)}.
       ```                                    |     | (35) |

The local kernel is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
q_{t\mid s}^{\mathrm{sym}}(y\mid z)=\big(1-\varepsilon_{s,t}\big)^{V-d_{H}(y,z)}\big(\varepsilon_{s,t}\big)^{d_{H}(y,z)}.
``` |  | (36) |

Using the odds $`\rho_{t}`$
from ([10](#S3.E10 "In Clean-conditioned reverse rates. ‣ 3.1 Binary symmetric diffusion ‣ 3 Binary discrete diffusion ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks"))
and writing $`z=Z_{t}^{i}`$, the reverse rates are

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle a_{i,u}^{\mathrm{sym}}(Z_{0},Z_{t};t)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2(1-t)}\begin{cases}\rho_{t},&z_{u}\neq(Z_{0}^{i})_{u},\\
\rho_{t}^{-1},&z_{u}=(Z_{0}^{i})_{u},\end{cases}`$ |  | (37) |
|  | $`\displaystyle a_{i,u}^{\theta,\mathrm{sym}}(Z_{t};t)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{\rho_{t}^{2z_{u}-1}}{2(1-t)}\frac{1+(\rho_{t}^{2}-1)\,\nu_{i}^{\theta}(z^{(u)}\mid Z_{t};t)}{1+(\rho_{t}^{2}-1)\,\nu_{i}^{\theta}(z\mid Z_{t};t)}.`$ |  |  |

###### Proof.

The bit-flip probability solves

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\partial_{t}\varepsilon_{s,t}=\frac{1-2\varepsilon_{s,t}}{2(1-t)},\qquad\varepsilon_{s,s}=0.
``` |  |

The stated flip probability satisfies this equation and initial
condition, and multiplying the independent bit kernels
proves ([36](#A2.E36 "In Proposition B.1 (Symmetric kernel and reverse rates). ‣ B.1 Binary symmetric diffusion ‣ Appendix B Mathematical details of binary diffusion ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")).
The clean-conditioned reverse rates follow from the change in Hamming
distance: a flip toward the clean bit multiplies the clean-conditioned
mass by $`\rho_{t}`$, while a flip away multiplies it by
$`\rho_{t}^{-1}`$. Multiplying these ratios by the forward flip rate
gives the formula for $`a_{i,u}`$.

To compute the model mass, put

|     |                                      |     |
|-----|--------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       C_{t}(z)=(1-t/2)^{V-|z|}(t/2)^{|z|}.
       ```                                   |     |

As a function of the clean token, the forward kernel is

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
q_{t\mid 0}(z\mid c)=C_{t}(z)\,\rho_{t}^{2z_{c}-1},\qquad m_{i}^{\theta}(z\mid Z_{t};t)=\frac{C_{t}(z)}{\rho_{t}}[1+(\rho_{t}^{2}-1)\,\nu_{i}^{\theta}(z\mid Z_{t};t)].
``` |  |

Toggling bit $`u`$ gives

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\frac{C_{t}(z^{(u)})}{C_{t}(z)}=\rho_{t}^{2z_{u}-1},\qquad\nu_{i}^{\theta}(z^{(u)}\mid Z_{t};t)=\nu_{i}^{\theta}(z\mid Z_{t};t)+(1-2z_{u})\,\mu_{i}^{\theta}(u\mid Z_{t};t).
``` |  |

The quotient of the two local masses, multiplied by $`1/[2(1-t)]`$,
gives the stated model rate. All local masses are positive for
$`0<t<1`$, so every bit flip has positive model rate. ∎

The denoiser used for decoding and sampling is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\pi_{i}^{\theta}(c\mid Z_{t};t)=\frac{\mu_{i}^{\theta}(c\mid Z_{t};t)\,\rho_{t}^{2(Z_{t}^{i})_{c}}}{1+(\rho_{t}^{2}-1)\,\nu_{i}^{\theta}(Z_{t}^{i}\mid Z_{t};t)}.
``` |  | (38) |

Substituting
$`\mu_{i}^{\theta}(u\mid Z_{t};t)=\rho_{t}^{-2z_{u}}\pi_{u}[1+(\rho_{t}^{2}-1)\nu_{i}^{\theta}(z\mid Z_{t};t)]`$,
with $`\pi_{u}=\pi_{i}^{\theta}(u\mid Z_{t};t)`$, turns the ratio of
masses
in ([37](#A2.E37 "In Proposition B.1 (Symmetric kernel and reverse rates). ‣ B.1 Binary symmetric diffusion ‣ Appendix B Mathematical details of binary diffusion ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks"))
into $`1-(1-\rho_{t}^{-2})\pi_{u}`$ for $`u\in z`$ and
$`1+(\rho_{t}^{2}-1)\pi_{u}`$ for $`u\notin z`$. The model rate is
therefore $`[\rho_{t}(1-\pi_{u})+\rho_{t}^{-1}\pi_{u}]/[2(1-t)]`$ for
removing an active candidate and
$`[\rho_{t}\pi_{u}+\rho_{t}^{-1}(1-\pi_{u})]/[2(1-t)]`$ for adding an
inactive one, which
is ([12](#S3.E12 "In Model reverse rates. ‣ 3.1 Binary symmetric diffusion ‣ 3 Binary discrete diffusion ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")).

#### Prior.

The prior draws independent fair bits,
$`p_{t_{2}}^{\mathrm{sym}}(z)=2^{-V}`$. For Bernoulli distributions with
success probabilities $`a,b\in(0,1)`$, the KL divergence is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
D_{\mathrm{Ber}}(a\|b)=a\log\frac{a}{b}+(1-a)\log\frac{1-a}{1-b}.
``` |  | (39) |

Conditional on the clean token $`c`$, the bits of $`Z_{t_{2}}^{i}`$ are
independent, with bit $`c`$ active with probability $`1-t_{2}/2`$ and
every other bit with probability $`t_{2}/2`$. The prior also factors
over bits, so the KL is a sum of Bernoulli terms, which coincide because
$`D_{\mathrm{Ber}}(1-a\|1/2)=D_{\mathrm{Ber}}(a\|1/2)`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\operatorname{KL}\big(q_{t_{2}\mid 0}^{\mathrm{sym}}(\cdot\mid c)\|p_{t_{2}}^{\mathrm{sym}}\big)=VD_{\mathrm{Ber}}(t_{2}/2\|1/2).
``` |  | (40) |

This does not depend on $`c`$ and vanishes as $`t_{2}\uparrow 1`$.

### B.2 Binary absorbing diffusion

###### Proposition B.2 (Absorbing kernel and rates).

Let each zero bit activate at rate $`1/(1-t)`$ and each active bit
remain active. For $`0\leq s<t<1`$ and nonempty binary vectors $`z,y`$,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
q_{t\mid s}^{\mathrm{abs}}(y\mid z)=\mathbf{1}\{z\subseteq y\}\left(\frac{1-t}{1-s}\right)^{V-|y|}\left(\frac{t-s}{1-s}\right)^{|y|-|z|}.
``` |  | (41) |

The expression is zero when the subset condition fails. For the clean
singleton $`\{c\}`$, it reduces to

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
q_{t\mid 0}^{\mathrm{abs}}(z\mid c)=\mathbf{1}\{c\in z\}(1-t)^{V-|z|}t^{|z|-1}.
``` |  | (42) |

The clean-conditioned and model reverse rates are

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
a_{i,u}^{\mathrm{abs}}(Z_{0},Z_{t};t)=\frac{\mathbf{1}\{u\in Z_{t}^{i}\setminus Z_{0}^{i}\}}{t},\qquad a_{i,u}^{\theta,\mathrm{abs}}(Z_{t};t)=\frac{\mathbf{1}\{u\in Z_{t}^{i}\}}{t}\frac{\nu_{i}^{\theta}(Z_{t}^{i}\setminus\{u\}\mid Z_{t};t)}{\nu_{i}^{\theta}(Z_{t}^{i}\mid Z_{t};t)}.
``` |  | (43) |

###### Proof.

A bit that is zero at $`s`$ remains zero at $`t`$ with probability

|     |                                                               |     |
|-----|---------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \exp\left(-\int_{s}^{t}\frac{dv}{1-v}\right)=\frac{1-t}{1-s}.
       ```                                                            |     |

Once activated, it remains one. Multiplication over bits
proves ([41](#A2.E41 "In Proposition B.2 (Absorbing kernel and rates). ‣ B.2 Binary absorbing diffusion ‣ Appendix B Mathematical details of binary diffusion ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")),
and $`z=\{c\}`$, $`s=0`$
gives ([42](#A2.E42 "In Proposition B.2 (Absorbing kernel and rates). ‣ B.2 Binary absorbing diffusion ‣ Appendix B Mathematical details of binary diffusion ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")).
For a nonempty state $`z`$,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
m_{i}^{\theta}(z\mid Z_{t};t)=(1-t)^{V-|z|}t^{|z|-1}\,\nu_{i}^{\theta}(z\mid Z_{t};t).
``` |  |

Deleting an active bit $`u`$ changes this mass by the factor

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\frac{(1-t)\,\nu_{i}^{\theta}(z\setminus\{u\}\mid Z_{t};t)}{t\,\nu_{i}^{\theta}(z\mid Z_{t};t)}.
``` |  |

Multiplying by the reversed forward activation rate $`1/(1-t)`$ gives
the model rate. For $`Z_{0}^{i}=c`$, the substitution

|     |                                                   |     |
|-----|---------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \mu_{i}^{\theta}(u\mid Z_{t};t)=\mathbf{1}\{u=c\}
       ```                                                |     |

gives the clean-conditioned rate. Deleting the last bit has zero rate
because the empty vector has zero mass. ∎

###### Proposition B.3 (Absorbing path loss).

Under the assumptions of
Proposition [B.2](#A2.Thmproposition2 "Proposition B.2 (Absorbing kernel and rates). ‣ B.2 Binary absorbing diffusion ‣ Appendix B Mathematical details of binary diffusion ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks"),

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{J}_{t}^{\mathrm{abs}}(\theta;Z_{0},Z_{t})=-\frac{1}{t}\sum_{i}\sum_{u\in Z_{t}^{i}\setminus Z_{0}^{i}}\log\left(1-\frac{\mu_{i}^{\theta}(u\mid Z_{t};t)}{\nu_{i}^{\theta}(Z_{t}^{i}\mid Z_{t};t)}\right).
``` |  | (44) |

###### Proof.

Fix $`i`$, write $`Z_{0}^{i}=c`$, and put

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
h_{u}=\frac{\mu_{i}^{\theta}(u\mid Z_{t};t)}{\nu_{i}^{\theta}(Z_{t}^{i}\mid Z_{t};t)},\quad u\in Z_{t}^{i},\qquad\sum_{u\in Z_{t}^{i}}h_{u}=1.
``` |  |

The homogeneity identity $`\Phi(a/t,b/t)=\Phi(a,b)/t`$ gives the local
loss times $`t`$ as

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Phi(0,1-h_{c})+\sum_{u\in Z_{t}^{i}\setminus\{c\}}\Phi(1,1-h_{u})=1-h_{c}+\sum_{u\neq c,\ u\in Z_{t}^{i}}[-h_{u}-\log(1-h_{u})].
``` |  |

Because the $`h_{u}`$ sum to one, the linear terms cancel,
leaving ([44](#A2.E44 "In Proposition B.3 (Absorbing path loss). ‣ B.2 Binary absorbing diffusion ‣ Appendix B Mathematical details of binary diffusion ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")).
For a singleton, the remaining sum is empty and the loss is zero. ∎

For absorbing diffusion, the local kernel is constant over clean tokens
in $`Z_{t}^{i}`$ and zero outside it. Bayes reweighting gives the
denoiser

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\pi_{i}^{\theta}(c\mid Z_{t};t)=\frac{\mu_{i}^{\theta}(c\mid Z_{t};t)\,\mathbf{1}\{c\in Z_{t}^{i}\}}{\nu_{i}^{\theta}(Z_{t}^{i}\mid Z_{t};t)}.
``` |  | (45) |

Since
$`\nu_{i}^{\theta}(Z_{t}^{i}\setminus\{u\}\mid Z_{t};t)/\nu_{i}^{\theta}(Z_{t}^{i}\mid Z_{t};t)=1-\pi_{i}^{\theta}(u\mid Z_{t};t)`$
for $`u\in Z_{t}^{i}`$, the model rate
in ([43](#A2.E43 "In Proposition B.2 (Absorbing kernel and rates). ‣ B.2 Binary absorbing diffusion ‣ Appendix B Mathematical details of binary diffusion ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks"))
equals ([14](#S3.E14 "In 3.2 Binary absorbing diffusion ‣ 3 Binary discrete diffusion ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")).
The cavity parameterization applies this support restriction
analytically, while a separately predicted denoiser must respect it
through explicit masking or learning.

### B.3 Binary ancestral bridges

By Bayes’ rule and the Markov property, the forward bridge of
Section [4](#S4 "4 Sampling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")
is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
q_{s\mid t,0}(y\mid z,c)=\frac{q_{t\mid s}(z\mid y)\,q_{s\mid 0}(y\mid c)}{q_{t\mid 0}(z\mid c)}.
``` |  | (46) |

Averaging it over the
denoiser ([5](#S2.E5 "In Training. ‣ 2 Discrete diffusion modeling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks"))
cancels $`q_{t\mid 0}(z\mid c)`$, which gives the plug-in form of the
ancestral
update ([18](#S4.E18 "In Ancestral sampling. ‣ 4 Sampling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")):

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
p_{s\mid t,i}^{\theta}(y\mid Z_{t})=\frac{q_{t\mid s}(Z_{t}^{i}\mid y)\sum_{c}\mu_{i}^{\theta}(c\mid Z_{t};t)\,q_{s\mid 0}(y\mid c)}{\sum_{c}\mu_{i}^{\theta}(c\mid Z_{t};t)\,q_{t\mid 0}(Z_{t}^{i}\mid c)}.
``` |  | (47) |

This is the bridge with the cavity in place of the clean token. We now
derive the conditional bit bridges
from ([46](#A2.E46 "In B.3 Binary ancestral bridges ‣ Appendix B Mathematical details of binary diffusion ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")).

#### Symmetric bridge.

Conditional on the clean proposal
$`\mathchoice{\widehat{Z}_{0}^{i}}{\smash[t]{\widehat{Z}_{0}^{i}}\vphantom{Z_{0}^{i}}}{\widehat{Z}_{0}^{i}}{\widehat{Z}_{0}^{i}}{}=c`$,
the bits are independent. With $`\varepsilon_{s,t}`$
from ([35](#A2.E35 "In Proposition B.1 (Symmetric kernel and reverse rates). ‣ B.1 Binary symmetric diffusion ‣ Appendix B Mathematical details of binary diffusion ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")),
bit $`u`$ with clean value $`b_{u}=\mathbf{1}\{u=c\}`$ and current value
$`z_{u}=(Z_{t}^{i})_{u}`$ differs from $`b_{u}`$ at $`s`$ with
probability

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
q^{\mathrm{sym}}\big((Z_{s}^{i})_{u}\neq b_{u}\mid z_{u},b_{u}\big)=\begin{cases}s\,\varepsilon_{s,t}/(2-t),&z_{u}=b_{u},\\[2.84526pt]
s\,(1-\varepsilon_{s,t})/t,&z_{u}\neq b_{u},\end{cases}
``` |  | (48) |

the chance of differing from the clean bit at $`s`$ and then flipping,
or not, to the current value at $`t`$. It favors the current value for
$`s`$ close to $`t`$ and the clean bit as $`s\downarrow 0`$.

A simpler symmetric sampler applies a one-bit Bayes update to each
cavity bit marginal and draws the bits independently. This ignores the
dependence between the bits through the shared clean token: at $`s=0`$,
the exact bridge draws a single one-hot state from $`\pi_{i}^{\theta}`$,
whereas independent bit draws can leave zero or several candidates
active. It performed worse in early experiments, and we dropped it.

#### Absorbing bridge.

Conditional on
$`\mathchoice{\widehat{Z}_{0}^{i}}{\smash[t]{\widehat{Z}_{0}^{i}}\vphantom{Z_{0}^{i}}}{\widehat{Z}_{0}^{i}}{\widehat{Z}_{0}^{i}}{}=c`$,
the bit $`c`$ stays active, and every bit inactive in $`Z_{t}^{i}`$
remains inactive at $`s`$. For $`u\in Z_{t}^{i}\setminus\{c\}`$,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
q^{\mathrm{abs}}((Z_{s}^{i})_{u}=1\mid(Z_{t}^{i})_{u}=1,Z_{0}^{i}=c)=\frac{s}{t}.
``` |  | (49) |

Indeed, a false candidate is active at $`s`$ with probability $`s`$,
active at $`t`$ with probability $`t`$, and activation by $`s`$ implies
activation by $`t`$. These bit events are independent conditional on
$`c`$ and the current state. The update therefore preserves nonemptiness
and produces a subset of the current active set.

## Appendix C Training objectives and time sampling

### C.1 Finite-window negative ELBO and boundary terms

The idealized
objective ([3](#S2.E3 "In 2 Discrete diffusion modeling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks"))
integrates the reverse process from clean data at $`t=0`$ to the
terminal noise distribution at $`t=1`$. In practice we use an interior
window $`0<t_{1}<t_{2}<1`$ to avoid singular jump rates near the
endpoints. The corresponding finite-window negative ELBO, abbreviated
NELBO in the appendices, is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\NELBO(\theta;t_{1},t_{2})=\mathcal{R}_{t_{1}}(\theta)+\mathcal{K}_{t_{2}}+\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\mathbb{E}_{Z_{0},Z_{t}}[\mathcal{J}_{t}(\theta;Z_{0},Z_{t})]\,dt,
``` |  | (50) |

where

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{R}_{t_{1}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{Z_{0},Z_{t_{1}}}[-\log p_{0\mid t_{1}}^{\theta}(Z_{0}\mid Z_{t_{1}})],\qquad\mathcal{K}_{t_{2}}=\mathbb{E}_{Z_{0}}\operatorname{KL}\big(q_{t_{2}\mid 0}(\cdot\mid Z_{0})\,\|\,p_{t_{2}}\big).
``` |  | (51) |

The first term, with the denoiser as decoder,
$`p_{0\mid t_{1}}^{\theta}(Z_{0}\mid Z_{t_{1}})=\prod_{i}\pi_{i}^{\theta}(Z_{0}^{i}\mid Z_{t_{1}};t_{1})`$,
accounts for the residual corruption at the clean end of the truncated
path, while the second measures the mismatch between the forward
distribution at $`t_{2}`$ and the prior from which generation starts.

For uniform and binary symmetric diffusion, the terminal-prior term is
finite and available analytically
(Apps. [A.2](#A1.SS2 "A.2 Uniform diffusion ‣ Appendix A Masked and uniform diffusion ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")
and [B.1](#A2.SS1 "B.1 Binary symmetric diffusion ‣ Appendix B Mathematical details of binary diffusion ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")).
With the prior matched to the limiting forward distribution, the
boundary contributions vanish as $`t_{1}\downarrow 0`$ and
$`t_{2}\uparrow 1`$,
recovering ([3](#S2.E3 "In 2 Discrete diffusion modeling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")).
For masked and binary absorbing diffusion, the limiting prior is a point
mass, so the terminal KL is infinite for every $`t_{2}<1`$ but zero at
$`t_{2}=1`$. The terminal endpoint therefore requires separate
treatment, and
App. [F.3](#A6.SS3.SSS0.Px1 "NELBO. ‣ F.3 Evaluation ‣ Appendix F Experimental details ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")
describes our likelihood-evaluation convention.

### C.2 Training objectives

Alongside the path ELBO, we compared a flat ELBO, cross-entropy (xent),
and weighted cross-entropy (wxent). For the kernels considered here, the
reverse rates share a scalar prefactor, which extends the flip rate
$`r_{t}`$
of ([9](#S3.E9 "In Forward rates. ‣ 3.1 Binary symmetric diffusion ‣ 3 Binary discrete diffusion ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks"))
to every kernel,

|     |                                                           |     |      |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       r_{t}=\begin{cases}1/[2(1-t)],&\text{binary symmetric},\\
       1/[V(1-t)],&\text{uniform},\\
       1/t,&\text{binary absorbing},\\
       1/t,&\text{masked},\end{cases}
       ```                                                        |     | (52) |

and the remaining factors are ratios of the forward kernel
$`q_{t\mid 0}`$ at the current noisy token. Since
$`\Phi(ra,rb)=r\Phi(a,b)`$, the prefactor is also the weight of the jump
penalties in the path integrand $`\mathcal{J}_{t}`$
of ([3](#S2.E3 "In 2 Discrete diffusion modeling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")).
The flat ELBO drops it,
$`\mathcal{J}_{t}^{\mathrm{flat}}=\mathcal{J}_{t}/r_{t}`$, which changes
the relative weight of the noise levels. Cross-entropy trains the
network output directly as a denoiser,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{J}_{t}^{\mathrm{xent}}(\theta;Z_{0},Z_{t})=-\sum_{i=1}^{L}\log\mu_{i}^{\theta}(Z_{0}^{i}\mid Z_{t};t),
``` |  | (53) |

and weighted cross-entropy multiplies it by the prefactor,
$`\mathcal{J}_{t}^{\mathrm{wxent}}=r_{t}\,\mathcal{J}_{t}^{\mathrm{xent}}`$.
For masked diffusion the sums run over masked positions. The ELBO and
wxent are integrated over time as
in ([3](#S2.E3 "In 2 Discrete diffusion modeling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")),
while the flat ELBO and xent are averaged over the base schedule of
App. [C.3](#A3.SS3 "C.3 Time schedules ‣ Appendix C Training objectives and time sampling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks").
All four are estimated with the inverse-density weight defined there,
which the adaptive proposal of
App. [C.5](#A3.SS5 "C.5 Adaptive gradient-RMS importance sampling ‣ Appendix C Training objectives and time sampling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")
preserves.

We train the logic models on the path ELBO. For text, we selected the
objective of each kernel and corpus on the validation NELBO after 10% of
the training budget. The path ELBO was best everywhere except on Text8,
where we train masked diffusion on xent, which coincides with its flat
ELBO, and binary absorbing diffusion on wxent. The latter still bounds
the likelihood, as we show next.

#### Absorbing cross-entropy bound.

For binary absorbing diffusion, wxent upper-bounds the path integrand.
Fix a position with clean token $`Z_{0}^{i}=c`$. The denoiser is
supported on the active set $`Z_{t}^{i}`$, which contains $`c`$, so

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\prod_{u\in Z_{t}^{i}\setminus\{c\}}\bigl(1-\pi_{i}^{\theta}(u\mid Z_{t};t)\bigr)\geq 1-\sum_{u\in Z_{t}^{i}\setminus\{c\}}\pi_{i}^{\theta}(u\mid Z_{t};t)=\pi_{i}^{\theta}(c\mid Z_{t};t).
``` |  | (54) |

Since
$`\pi_{i}^{\theta}(c\mid Z_{t};t)=\mu_{i}^{\theta}(c\mid Z_{t};t)/\nu_{i}^{\theta}(Z_{t}^{i}\mid Z_{t};t)\geq\mu_{i}^{\theta}(c\mid Z_{t};t)`$,
taking negative logarithms, multiplying by $`1/t`$, and summing over
positions
in ([44](#A2.E44 "In Proposition B.3 (Absorbing path loss). ‣ B.2 Binary absorbing diffusion ‣ Appendix B Mathematical details of binary diffusion ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks"))
gives
$`\mathcal{J}_{t}^{\mathrm{abs}}\leq\mathcal{J}_{t}^{\mathrm{wxent}}`$.

### C.3 Time schedules

The base schedule reparameterizes corruption time on the clipped window
$`[t_{1},t_{2}]`$ by $`\xi\in[0,1]`$, which we draw uniformly during
training. The linear, logarithmic, and cosine maps are

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
t_{\mathrm{lin}}(\xi)=t_{1}+(t_{2}-t_{1})\xi,\qquad t_{\log}(\xi)=t_{1}\left(\frac{t_{2}}{t_{1}}\right)^{\xi},\qquad t_{\cos}(\xi)=t_{1}+(t_{2}-t_{1})\sin^{2}\!\Big(\frac{\pi\xi}{2}\Big),
``` |  | (55) |

which give the base sampling densities on $`[t_{1},t_{2}]`$

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
p_{\mathrm{lin}}(t)=\frac{1}{t_{2}-t_{1}},\qquad p_{\log}(t)=\frac{1}{t\log(t_{2}/t_{1})},\qquad p_{\cos}(t)=\frac{1}{\pi\sqrt{(t-t_{1})(t_{2}-t)}}.
``` |  | (56) |

Logarithmic sampling assigns equal probability to intervals with the
same ratio of endpoints, giving more resolution near clean data. At
large vocabularies, this matches how the binary kernels lose information
(App. [C.4](#A3.SS4 "C.4 Information retained under each kernel ‣ Appendix C Training objectives and time sampling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")).
Cosine sampling instead gives more resolution near both ends of the
window. To estimate the path integral without bias, we weight each
sequence’s loss by the inverse density of its sampled time, namely
$`t_{2}-t_{1}`$ for the linear schedule, $`t\log(t_{2}/t_{1})`$ for the
logarithmic schedule, and $`\pi\sqrt{(t-t_{1})(t_{2}-t)}`$ for the
cosine schedule.

We give $`\xi`$ to the network as its time input:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\xi(t)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{t-t_{1}}{t_{2}-t_{1}},&\text{linear schedule},\\[6.0pt]
\displaystyle\frac{\log(t/t_{1})}{\log(t_{2}/t_{1})},&\text{logarithmic schedule},\\[6.0pt]
\displaystyle\frac{2}{\pi}\arcsin\sqrt{\frac{t-t_{1}}{t_{2}-t_{1}}},&\text{cosine schedule}.\end{cases}
``` |  | (57) |

The adaptive proposal below also acts on $`\xi`$, while the kernel and
rates retain their definitions in corruption time $`t`$. We choose
inference grids separately from training-time sampling. Applying any map
in ([55](#A3.E55 "In C.3 Time schedules ‣ Appendix C Training objectives and time sampling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks"))
to $`j/N`$, for $`j=0,\ldots,N`$, gives a linear, logarithmic, or cosine
grid for $`N`$ reverse steps, traversed in decreasing $`j`$ as in
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ Confidence-guided Ψ-sampler. ‣ 4 Sampling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks").
The logarithmic grid has smaller absolute steps near $`t_{1}`$, and the
cosine grid near both ends of the window. We train with the linear and
logarithmic schedules
(Tables [3](#A6.T3 "Table 3 ‣ F.1 Optimization details ‣ Appendix F Experimental details ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")
and [4](#A6.T4 "Table 4 ‣ F.1 Optimization details ‣ Appendix F Experimental details ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks"))
and sample on grids of all three kinds
(Table [7](#A6.T7 "Table 7 ‣ F.4 Sampler tuning procedure ‣ Appendix F Experimental details ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")).

### C.4 Information retained under each kernel

Section [3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Information loss and the time schedule ‣ 3 Binary discrete diffusion ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")
and
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3.4 Information loss and the time schedule ‣ 3 Binary discrete diffusion ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")
consider independent positions whose clean tokens are uniform on
$`[V]`$. The other positions then carry no information about
$`Z_{0}^{i}`$, so the true cavity is uniform,
$`q(Z_{0}^{i}=c\mid Z_{t}^{-i})=1/V`$, and the information in the noisy
sequence is a sum over positions of

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
I(Z_{0}^{i};Z_{t}^{i})=\log V-\mathbb{E}\,\big[H\big(q(Z_{0}^{i}\mid Z_{t}^{i})\big)\big],
``` |  | (58) |

where the posterior of the clean token is the
denoiser ([5](#S2.E5 "In Training. ‣ 2 Discrete diffusion modeling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks"))
with a uniform $`\mu_{i}^{\theta}`$, the forward kernel
$`q_{t\mid 0}(Z_{t}^{i}\mid c)`$ normalized over $`c`$.

- •
  Masked. The posterior is a point mass at an unmasked token and uniform
  at a mask, so $`I=(1-t)\log V`$.
- •
  Uniform. Given the noisy token, the posterior assigns $`a=1-t+t/V`$ to
  it and $`b=t/V`$ to every other token, so
  $`I=\log V+a\log a+(V-1)\,b\log b`$.
- •
  Binary absorbing. The posterior is uniform on the active set, whose
  size is $`1+K`$ with $`K\sim\mathrm{Bin}(V-1,t)`$, so
  $`I=\log V-\mathbb{E}[\log(1+K)]\geq\log V-\log(1+(V-1)t)`$ by
  Jensen’s inequality.
- •
  Binary symmetric. A state $`z`$ differs from the clean token $`c`$ in
  $`d_{H}(z,c)=|z|+1-2z_{c}`$ bits, so the likelihood
  $`q_{t\mid 0}^{\mathrm{sym}}(z\mid c)`$ is proportional to
  $`\rho_{t}^{-d_{H}(z,c)}\propto\rho_{t}^{2z_{c}}`$ as a function of
  $`c`$, and with a uniform prior the posterior weighs active candidates
  by $`\rho_{t}^{2}`$ and inactive tokens by one,
  as ([38](#A2.E38 "In B.1 Binary symmetric diffusion ‣ Appendix B Mathematical details of binary diffusion ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks"))
  with a uniform $`\mu_{i}^{\theta}`$. A state with $`k`$ active
  candidates therefore has posterior entropy

  |  |  |  |  |
  |----|----|----|----|
  |  |
  ``` math
  H_{k}=\log(k\rho_{t}^{2}+V-k)-\frac{k\rho_{t}^{2}\log\rho_{t}^{2}}{k\rho_{t}^{2}+V-k},
  ``` |  | (59) |

  and $`I=\log V-\mathbb{E}H_{B+K}`$ with independent
  $`B\sim\mathrm{Ber}(1-t/2)`$, the clean bit, and
  $`K\sim\mathrm{Bin}(V-1,t/2)`$, the false candidates. For small $`t`$,
  $`\rho_{t}^{2}`$ is large and the posterior is nearly uniform on the
  active set, so that $`I\approx\log V-\log(1+(V-1)t/2)`$, as in the
  absorbing case with half as many false candidates.

These expressions give the curves of
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3.4 Information loss and the time schedule ‣ 3 Binary discrete diffusion ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks").
With $`V=1024`$ on the window $`[5\cdot 10^{-4},0.9999]`$, the linear
schedule draws 95% of its times where less than half of the information
is left under binary symmetric diffusion and 97% under binary absorbing
diffusion, against 50% under masked and 60% under uniform diffusion. The
logarithmic schedule lowers these fractions to 39% and 46% for the
binary kernels. On the other hand, with $`V=9`$, half of the information
is lost at $`t\approx 0.27`$ under binary symmetric, $`0.28`$ under
binary absorbing, and $`0.29`$ under uniform diffusion, so the binary
kernels lose information about as fast as uniform diffusion.

### C.5 Adaptive gradient-RMS importance sampling

Adaptive importance sampling replaces the base schedule by a proposal
that draws more samples where loss gradients are large. It improved over
the base schedule alone in all our experiments, so we train every model,
for all four kernels and all tasks, with it. The statistic is the
root-mean-square norm of the gradient with respect to the network’s
output logits, used as an inexpensive proxy for parameter-gradient
norms.

We divide the range of $`\xi`$ into $`K=32`$ equal-width bins. Let
$`g_{\theta}`$ denote a sequence’s contribution to the loss under the
base schedule, including token normalization and the base-schedule
weight, and let $`\ell`$ denote its output logits. For the path
objective with $`L`$ scored tokens per sequence, this contribution is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
g_{\theta}=\frac{\mathcal{J}_{t}(\theta;Z_{0},Z_{t})}{L\,p_{\mathrm{base}}(t)},\qquad p_{\mathrm{base}}\in\{p_{\mathrm{lin}},p_{\log},p_{\cos}\}.
``` |  | (60) |

When scored token counts vary across sequences, we replace $`L`$ by
their minibatch mean. In each bin $`k`$, we maintain exponentially
decayed sums $`S_{k}`$ of $`\|\nabla_{\ell}g_{\theta}\|_{2}^{2}`$ and
counts $`C_{k}`$, both with decay $`0.99`$. Their ratio gives the mean
squared gradient norm, from which we form the RMS estimate and the bin
probability:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
G_{k}=\sqrt{\frac{S_{k}}{C_{k}}},\qquad P_{k}=0.9\frac{G_{k}}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}G_{j}}+\frac{0.1}{K}.
``` |  | (61) |

Sampling uniformly within each selected bin gives the time density and
path-loss weight

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
p(t)=KP_{k}\,p_{\mathrm{base}}(t),\qquad\frac{1}{p(t)}=\frac{1}{KP_{k}\,p_{\mathrm{base}}(t)},\qquad\xi(t)\text{ in bin }k.
``` |  | (62) |

The additional factor $`1/(KP_{k})`$ preserves the objective under the
base schedule. Mixing in $`10\%`$ of the base schedule keeps every bin
accessible and bounds this factor by $`10`$.

For the first 100 minibatches we sample from the base schedule while
collecting statistics. Each minibatch uses the preceding proposal, held
fixed during differentiation, and updates the statistics for the next
minibatch. We stratify the times within a minibatch in the proposal’s
cumulative-probability coordinate. For validation, we draw times from
the base schedule.

## Appendix D Confidence-guided $`\Psi`$-sampler

This appendix specifies each setting of
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ Confidence-guided Ψ-sampler. ‣ 4 Sampling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")
for all four kernels. One step maps the state $`Z_{t}`$ to $`Z_{s}`$,
$`s<t`$, on a sampling grid with linear, cosine, or logarithmic spacing
(App. [C.3](#A3.SS3 "C.3 Time schedules ‣ Appendix C Training objectives and time sampling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")).
We hold conditioning positions, such as Sudoku clues, fixed and exclude
them from every average over positions below.

#### Temperature $`T`$ and nucleus top-$`p`$.

For every draw from the denoiser, for the clean proposal, inside the
ancestral update, and in the final decoding, we use the tempered
denoiser

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\pi_{i}^{\theta,T}(c\mid Z_{t};t)\propto\pi_{i}^{\theta}(c\mid Z_{t};t)^{1/T},
``` |  | (63) |

which on text we further restrict to its top-$`p`$ nucleus and
renormalize, and $`T=0`$ selects the most probable token. The clean
proposal
$`\mathchoice{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}{\smash[t]{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}\vphantom{Z_{0}^{i}}}{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}{}\sim\pi_{i}^{\theta,T}(\cdot\mid Z_{t};t)`$
is drawn independently at each position, and the ancestral update draws
its own proposal
$`\mathchoice{\widehat{Z}_{0}^{i}}{\smash[t]{\widehat{Z}_{0}^{i}}\vphantom{Z_{0}^{i}}}{\widehat{Z}_{0}^{i}}{\widehat{Z}_{0}^{i}}{}`$
in the same way.

#### Re-corrupt fraction $`\eta`$.

Each position is re-corrupted with probability $`\kappa_{i}`$ and
otherwise takes the ancestral
update ([18](#S4.E18 "In Ancestral sampling. ‣ 4 Sampling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")),
as
in ([21](#S4.E21 "In Confidence-guided Ψ-sampler. ‣ 4 Sampling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")).
Without position confidence, $`\kappa_{i}=\eta`$ at every position, so
that $`\eta=0`$ is ancestral sampling and $`\eta=1`$ re-corrupts every
position at every step.

#### Confidence coordinate.

Position confidence and the ordering tilt read the confidence in the
proposal from the cavity or from the denoiser,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{conf}_{i}=\mu_{i}^{\theta}(\mathchoice{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}{\smash[t]{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}\vphantom{Z_{0}^{i}}}{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}{}\mid Z_{t};t)\qquad\text{or}\qquad\mathrm{conf}_{i}=\pi_{i}^{\theta}(\mathchoice{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}{\smash[t]{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}\vphantom{Z_{0}^{i}}}{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}{}\mid Z_{t};t).
``` |  | (64) |

The cavity reflects the context alone, while the denoiser also accounts
for the position’s own noisy state.

#### Position confidence $`\gamma`$.

The re-corruption probabilities decrease with confidence,

|     |                                                               |     |      |
|-----|---------------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \kappa_{i}=\min\{1,\,\zeta\,e^{-\gamma\,\mathrm{conf}_{i}}\},
       ```                                                            |     | (65) |

where we set the constant $`\zeta`$ by bisection so that the mean of
$`\kappa_{i}`$ over positions equals $`\eta`$. Positions capped at one
thus pass their excess to the others, and $`\gamma=0`$ gives
$`\kappa_{i}=\eta`$. For masked diffusion, masked positions keep
$`\kappa_{i}=\eta`$, and the redistribution runs over the unmasked
positions only, each with the confidence in its token recorded when it
was unmasked, since the network is not trained at unmasked positions.

#### Ordering tilt $`\lambda`$.

A re-corrupted position returns to its own noise level

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
s_{i}=\min\{1,\,\zeta^{\prime}\,e^{-\lambda\,\mathrm{conf}_{i}}\}
``` |  | (66) |

instead of $`s`$, with $`\zeta^{\prime}`$ set so that the mean of
$`s_{i}`$ over positions equals $`s`$. Less confident positions are thus
corrupted more while the mean noise level follows the grid, and
$`\lambda=0`$ gives $`s_{i}=s`$.

#### Candidate confidence $`\beta`$.

Plain re-corruption opens alternatives uniformly at random, as the
forward kernel does. With candidate confidence, the binary kernels
corrupt the proposal’s own bit as the forward kernel does, dropping it
with probability $`s_{i}/2`$ under binary symmetric diffusion and
keeping it under binary absorbing diffusion, and open each other token
$`u\neq\mathchoice{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}{\smash[t]{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}\vphantom{Z_{0}^{i}}}{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}{}`$
independently with probability $`\min\{1,\zeta_{i}\,p_{i,u}^{\beta}\}`$,
where $`\zeta_{i}`$ is set so that

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\sum_{u\neq\mathchoice{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}{\smash[t]{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}\vphantom{Z_{0}^{i}}}{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}{}}\min\{1,\,\zeta_{i}\,p_{i,u}^{\beta}\}=\begin{cases}(V-1)s_{i}/2,&\text{binary symmetric},\\
(V-1)s_{i},&\text{binary absorbing}.\end{cases}
``` |  | (67) |

The expected number of opened alternatives is thus that of the forward
kernel, which $`\beta=0`$ recovers. The weight $`p_{i,u}`$ is the
denoiser probability of $`u`$ at the most recent step at which $`u`$ was
a candidate at position $`i`$, starting from $`1/V`$, because the binary
absorbing denoiser vanishes outside the current set. Without this
memory, reopening in proportion to the current cavity or denoiser
probability lowers binary symmetric diffusion’s best Sudoku validation
solve rate over the same grid to 89.6% and 85.2%, below position
confidence alone (95.2%). Uniform diffusion re-corrupts a position by
changing its token with the forward probability $`(V-1)s_{i}/V`$ and
draws the new token
$`u\neq\mathchoice{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}{\smash[t]{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}\vphantom{Z_{0}^{i}}}{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}{\widetilde{Z}_{0}^{i}}{}`$
with probability proportional to
$`\pi_{i}^{\theta}(u\mid Z_{t};t)^{\beta}`$, so that $`\beta=0`$ is
again the forward kernel. Masked diffusion has no candidate to reopen.

#### Final decoding.

After the last step, we decode each position from the tempered denoiser
at $`t_{1}`$, keeping the unmasked tokens of masked diffusion.

## Appendix E Extended related work

#### Discrete diffusion and corruption-state design.

Several lines of work broaden the forward path without introducing
candidate sets. Generalized interpolating diffusion and kinetic path
design admit richer categorical couplings ([von Rütte et al.,
2025](#bib.bib56); [Shaul et al., 2025](#bib.bib47)), partial masking
inserts intermediate corruption states between a token and a full
mask ([Chao et al., 2025](#bib.bib8)), and sticky jump processes combine
discrete jumps with continuous coordinates ([Jutras-Dubé et al.,
2026](#bib.bib26)). CADD and CANDI go further and augment or hybridize
the categorical state with a continuous one ([Zheng et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib64); [Pynadath et al., 2025](#bib.bib37)). Even at scale,
and with architectures and training budgets matched, the choice between
masking, uniform corruption, and interpolating paths remains
consequential ([Sahoo et al., 2026](#bib.bib42)).

There is also a substantial simplex-valued lineage, which lifts
categories to continuous points on the simplex or updates distribution
parameters directly ([Richemond et al., 2022](#bib.bib39); [Floto
et al., 2023](#bib.bib15); [Avdeyev et al., 2023](#bib.bib2); [Stärk
et al., 2024](#bib.bib51); [Graves et al., 2023](#bib.bib20); [Chandra
et al., 2026](#bib.bib7)). Simplax is the closest of these to our
setting: it keeps uniform categorical diffusion as its marginal and adds
an exact Dirichlet auxiliary variable to the reverse bridge ([Sakurai
et al., 2026](#bib.bib43)). Its denoiser, however, still observes a
corrupted category, whereas binary diffusion exposes the candidate set
to the denoiser as the noisy state.

#### Binary diffusion and candidate-set representations.

Prior binary diffusion methods treat each bit as part of the object
being generated. Bit-flip diffusion of binary data goes back to binomial
diffusion ([Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015](#bib.bib49)), and DMPM studies
its continuous-time form ([Pham et al., 2025](#bib.bib35)). BerDiff
applies a Bernoulli kernel to binary segmentation masks ([Chen et al.,
2023a](#bib.bib9)), GraphGUIDE adds, removes, or flips graph edges
through Bernoulli transitions ([Tseng et al., 2023](#bib.bib55)), and
Blackout diffusion models discrete counts through birth–death
processes ([Santos et al., 2023](#bib.bib44)). Analog Bits instead
encodes one category in $`\lceil\log_{2}V\rceil`$ real-valued bit
coordinates and applies continuous diffusion ([Chen et al.,
2023b](#bib.bib10)). In binary diffusion, by contrast, there are $`V`$
binary coordinates per position and an active bit denotes membership in
the noisy subset.

The ShortListing Model (SLM) is the closest predecessor ([Song et al.,
2025](#bib.bib50)). It represents a categorical variable by a nonempty
candidate set, starts the forward process from the clean singleton,
activates false candidates until reaching the full vocabulary, and
samples in reverse by progressive candidate pruning. However, the model
is formulated in discrete time and identifies sets with simplex-face
centroids. To see the correspondence with binary absorbing diffusion,
let $`n_{t}`$ be SLM’s expected candidate-set size at time $`t`$ and
take the linear noise schedule

|     |                 |     |      |
|-----|-----------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       n_{t}=1+(V-1)t.
       ```              |     | (68) |

The probability of adding a candidate between times $`s<t`$ is then

|     |                                              |     |      |
|-----|----------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \frac{n_{t}-n_{s}}{V-n_{s}}=\frac{t-s}{1-s},
       ```                                           |     | (69) |

and the clean-conditioned probability of retaining a false candidate is

|     |                                      |     |      |
|-----|--------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \frac{n_{s}-1}{n_{t}-1}=\frac{s}{t},
       ```                                   |     | (70) |

which are the absorbing
kernel ([41](#A2.E41 "In Proposition B.2 (Absorbing kernel and rates). ‣ B.2 Binary absorbing diffusion ‣ Appendix B Mathematical details of binary diffusion ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks"))
and
bridge ([49](#A2.E49 "In Absorbing bridge. ‣ B.3 Binary ancestral bridges ‣ Appendix B Mathematical details of binary diffusion ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")).

#### Diffusion for structured reasoning.

Beyond Autoregression established masked diffusion baselines on Sudoku
and other reasoning and planning tasks ([Ye et al., 2025](#bib.bib62)).
Dirichlet diffusion solves Sudoku in a continuous simplex
state ([Avdeyev et al., 2023](#bib.bib2)), and Simplax reports Sudoku
generalization across clue densities ([Sakurai et al.,
2026](#bib.bib43)). Several analyses show that the corruption and the
order of updates matter as much as the model: Spatial Reasoning Models
find that the order of variable updates strongly affects
accuracy ([Wewer et al., 2025](#bib.bib60)), and the locality induced by
the corruption and factorization changes trainability on Sudoku and
graph path-finding ([Wang et al., 2026](#bib.bib59)). On the theoretical
side, masked diffusion models can simulate chain-of-thought under finite
precision ([Svete & Sabharwal, 2026](#bib.bib53)).

A separate line of work changes the reverse-time policy rather than the
forward state, through token ordering, planned denoising and path
planning, remasking, learned reveal schedules, or search during and
around sampling ([Kim et al., 2025](#bib.bib27); [Liu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib30); [Peng et al., 2025](#bib.bib34); [Wang et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib58); [Kim et al., 2026](#bib.bib28); [Xu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib61); [Ta et al., 2026](#bib.bib54); [Bai et al.,
2026](#bib.bib3); [Zhang et al., 2026](#bib.bib63)). These methods
compose with any corruption kernel, and beyond the confidence-guided
re-corruption of
Section [4](#S4 "4 Sampling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")
we use none of them: our verifier-free solve rate refers to direct
samples from each kernel’s tuned sampler, without search, reranking, or
a symbolic solver.

#### Recurrent reasoning.

Sudoku and related benchmarks have also driven a rapidly growing
literature on small recurrent reasoners, which allocate computation
through repeated latent updates, fixed-point dynamics, or looped
layers ([Wang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib57); [Jolicoeur-Martineau,
2025](#bib.bib25); [Sghaier et al., 2026](#bib.bib46); [Huang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib24); [Fein-Ashley & Rashidinejad, 2026](#bib.bib14);
[Helbling et al., 2026](#bib.bib22); [Cameron et al., 2026](#bib.bib4);
[Lee et al., 2026](#bib.bib29)). These approaches change the
architecture, the training dynamics, or the recurrent depth, which is a
separate axis from the corruption state that binary diffusion changes,
so we do not compare against them directly.

### F.2 Learning-rate and checkpoint selection

We selected the learning rate of each task and kernel from
$`\{10^{-4},3\cdot 10^{-4},10^{-3}\}`$ on the validation NELBO of
App. [F.3](#A6.SS3.SSS0.Px1 "NELBO. ‣ F.3 Evaluation ‣ Appendix F Experimental details ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks"),
computed on 51,200 validation draws and averaged over two training seeds
(Table [5](#A6.T5 "Table 5 ‣ F.2 Learning-rate and checkpoint selection ‣ Appendix F Experimental details ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")).
Within each task, kernel, and seed, all learning rates share the data,
times, and corruptions, so their differences have a Monte Carlo standard
error below $`3\cdot 10^{-4}`$, and the variation between seeds
dominates. We tune Sudoku and graph coloring at their full training
budget and Boxoban at 1M steps. On Boxoban uniform and binary absorbing,
the two lowest learning rates are within seed noise, and in both cases
we keep the middle rate $`3\cdot 10^{-4}`$. Since Boxoban validation
NELBO was still improving slowly at that point, we trained the selected
rates for 2.5M steps and selected a checkpoint for each run on the
validation NELBO, evaluated every 100k steps from 1M. We keep the final
checkpoint unless an earlier one is lower by more than two standard
errors of the paired difference, and only two binary absorbing seeds
select an earlier checkpoint, at 2.0M and 1.0M steps.

### F.3 Evaluation

#### NELBO.

We evaluate the finite-window
NELBO ([50](#A3.E50 "In C.1 Finite-window negative ELBO and boundary terms ‣ Appendix C Training objectives and time sampling ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks"))
on the training window with the estimators used in training. For the
path term, we draw one time per sequence from the training time schedule
with inverse-density weighting. We estimate reconstruction from forward
corruptions at $`t_{1}`$ with the denoiser as decoder, and visible
tokens in masked diffusion are copied exactly and have zero
reconstruction loss. The prior is the limiting distribution from which
generation starts. Its KL from the time-$`t_{2}`$ corruption is analytic
for uniform and binary symmetric diffusion
(Apps. [A.2](#A1.SS2 "A.2 Uniform diffusion ‣ Appendix A Masked and uniform diffusion ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")
and [B.1](#A2.SS1 "B.1 Binary symmetric diffusion ‣ Appendix B Mathematical details of binary diffusion ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")).
For masked and binary absorbing diffusion the prior is a point mass, so
that the KL is infinite for $`t_{2}<1`$ and zero at $`t_{2}=1`$, and we
omit it. We aggregate the total NELBO over scored tokens, excluding
padding and conditioning clues.

#### Logic solve rate.

We score logic models on direct samples, with one attempt per instance
and no verifier or selection among attempts, so the reported solve rate
is single-attempt success. Sudoku success requires the completed
reference grid, and Boxoban success requires legal actions that end with
every box on a goal, with the action sequence read up to the first STAY,
the no-operation action that pads solutions. Graph coloring accepts any
proper coloring. We evaluate the selected EMA checkpoint of each of the
five training seeds
(App. [F.2](#A6.SS2 "F.2 Learning-rate and checkpoint selection ‣ Appendix F Experimental details ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks"))
with a linear sampling grid on $`[0.01,0.9999]`$ and the sampler
selected on validation at the reference NFE, 256 for Sudoku and Boxoban
and 64 for graph coloring
(App. [F.4](#A6.SS4 "F.4 Sampler tuning procedure ‣ Appendix F Experimental details ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")).
The tables use the full test splits, and the NFE and training curves use
8,192 and 4,096 test instances, except in their hard columns, which use
every hard test instance. We evaluate every kernel on the same instances
and fix the difficulty bins on validation data. The hard subsets are
defined with the data in
App. [F.5](#A6.SS5 "F.5 Logic tasks ‣ Appendix F Experimental details ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks").
We report the mean and standard error over training seeds.

#### Text sample quality.

We tune every sampler setting on the validation split and evaluate on
the test split of each corpus
(App. [F.6](#A6.SS6 "F.6 Language modeling ‣ Appendix F Experimental details ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")).
After removing special tokens, we retokenize complete decoded strings
with GPT-2 Large for GenPPL and MAUVE features. Each sample set holds
2,000 samples from one generation seed, and each reported value averages
the two generation seeds of a sampler setting. Entropy is the unigram
entropy, in nats, of the GPT-2 tokens pooled over a sample set rather
than a within-string average, so it measures the diversity of the set as
a whole. GenPPL is the exponential of the total GPT-2 Large negative
log-likelihood of the sample set divided by its total token count, so it
is pooled over tokens rather than averaged over strings. We compute
MAUVE with 200 buckets and average it over four reference draws and five
clustering seeds, with reference subsets sampled without replacement and
of the size of the generated sample set. Error bars span the two
generation seeds and condition on the checkpoint.

### F.4 Sampler tuning procedure

We sample every kernel with the confidence-guided $`\Psi`$-sampler of
App. [D](#A4 "Appendix D Confidence-guided Ψ-sampler ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks").
Its settings are the temperature $`T`$, the re-corrupt fraction
$`\eta`$, the confidence coordinate, the position-confidence strength
$`\gamma`$, the ordering tilt $`\lambda`$, and the candidate-confidence
strength $`\beta`$, which we tune for every kernel but masked diffusion
on the logic tasks and for the binary kernels on text. On text, we also
tune the nucleus top-$`p`$ and the spacing of the sampling grid. We
apply temperature and top-$`p`$ to the denoiser rather than to the
cavity ([Casado Noguerales et al., 2026](#bib.bib6)).

For each task and kernel, we select these settings on validation over
the grids of
Table [7](#A6.T7 "Table 7 ‣ F.4 Sampler tuning procedure ‣ Appendix F Experimental details ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks").
On the logic tasks the score is the mean solve rate over the training
seeds on a fixed validation split of 2,048 instances (1,024 for the
large graphs) at the reference NFE. On text it is MAUVE at NFE $`=L`$,
screened with 512 samples and confirmed with 2,000 samples for the three
best candidates. We then freeze the selection for every test
measurement, budget, and training seed unless otherwise stated. We
select the sampler of the hard columns separately on the hard subsets of
the validation splits. The grids are not full products: the ordering and
confidence strengths enter through a few sub-grids, and we give masked
diffusion, which has no candidate to reopen, a matching number of extra
ordering and re-corruption points in place of the candidate-confidence
settings
(Table [7](#A6.T7 "Table 7 ‣ F.4 Sampler tuning procedure ‣ Appendix F Experimental details ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")),
so we tune every kernel with the same budget. Because the cavity and the
denoiser coincide for masked diffusion, the confidence coordinate has no
effect there.
Table [10](#A6.T10 "Table 10 ‣ F.4 Sampler tuning procedure ‣ Appendix F Experimental details ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")
selects over nested subsets of the logic grid: ancestral sampling,
re-corruption alone, the $`\Psi`$-sampler without confidence, with
position confidence, and with every setting, so each row reports what
its settings add. Candidate confidence lifts binary symmetric diffusion
on Sudoku and binary absorbing diffusion on the large graphs, whereas it
is only selected for uniform diffusion on the Boxoban hard subset.
Tables [8](#A6.T8 "Table 8 ‣ F.4 Sampler tuning procedure ‣ Appendix F Experimental details ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")
and [9](#A6.T9 "Table 9 ‣ F.4 Sampler tuning procedure ‣ Appendix F Experimental details ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")
list the selected settings.

Figure [4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 5.2 Text ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")
measures each kernel at several entropies: we bin the sampler settings
screened on validation by GPT-2 token entropy, evaluate the best of each
bin on the test split with 2,000 samples and two generation seeds, and
draw the upper envelope of these points over entropy, on which the
validation-selected setting lies for every kernel.

### F.5 Logic tasks

In every task, we condition the model on the given part of the instance:
we show it clean, never corrupt it, and exclude it from the loss, so all
randomness and revision act on the generated positions.

#### Sudoku.

For Sudoku, we use the Sudoku-Extreme boards of [Wang et al.
(2025a)](#bib.bib57), 3.8M training boards and a test pool of 423k, as
81 digit tokens with the clue cells fixed. We mark the clue cells with
an embedding added to the input. This changed little for the masked and
binary kernels but was necessary for uniform diffusion to train at all,
since a clue is otherwise indistinguishable from a uniformly corrupted
cell. We partition the test pool into validation and test sets of about
200k and 223k boards that are orbit-disjoint under the augmentation
symmetries (digit relabeling, board flips, and rotations), and the hard
subset of the test set keeps the boards with at most 22 clues (4.1%).

#### Boxoban.

For Boxoban, we use the $`10\times 10`$ levels of [Guez et al.
(2018)](#bib.bib21) with the A^(⋆) solutions of [Garriga-Alonso et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib17) and keep the levels whose solution replays to a
solved board. Each sequence is the flattened board followed by 128
action tokens, the solution padded with STAY, and we score the whole
action region. Because the official test pool holds only 1,000 levels,
we partition the 92k solved levels of the official validation pool once
into validation and test sets of 25k levels each and fold the remaining
42k into the 936k training levels, and the hard subset keeps the boards
whose solution needs at least 40 moves (19.8%).

#### Graph coloring.

Graph coloring instances are random graphs with a planted four-coloring:
64 vertices in four balanced color classes, with each cross-class edge
present independently with probability $`0.2`$, so the mean degree is
$`9.6`$, just above the Kesten–Stigum threshold $`(k-1)^{2}=9`$ for
$`k=4`$ colors, below which the planted coloring is undetectable. Any
proper coloring counts as a solution, not only the planted one. We pass
the graph’s adjacency matrix to the model as an attention mask and
generate instances on the fly from separate seeded streams for training,
validation (2,048 instances), and test (100k). The hard subset consists
of 4,096 graphs of 640 vertices at the same mean degree, with the edge
probability scaled to $`0.02`$.

During training, we augment Sudoku with the symmetries above and Boxoban
with joint board and action rotations and reflections, while validation
and test examples are unaugmented.
Figure [5](#A6.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ Graph coloring. ‣ F.5 Logic tasks ‣ Appendix F Experimental details ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")
gives the solve rate by difficulty bin and by graph size.

Figure 5: Solve rate by difficulty at the reference NFE, harder to the
right: Sudoku by the number of clues, Boxoban by the length of the
reference solution, and graph coloring by graph size at a fixed mean
degree.

### F.6 Language modeling

For all text models, we use the diffusion transformer of [Sahoo et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib40) with time conditioning, with about 92M non-embedding
parameters on Text8 and TinyStories and 214M on OpenWebText, and train
every run on 131B tokens.
Table [4](#A6.T4 "Table 4 ‣ F.1 Optimization details ‣ Appendix F Experimental details ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")
lists the remaining training settings.

#### Text8.

Text8 ([Mahoney, 2011](#bib.bib32)) is the first $`10^{8}`$ characters
of a cleaned English Wikipedia dump, over 27 characters, in sequences of
$`L=256`$. We use the standard split into the first 90M characters for
training and 5M each for validation and test.

#### TinyStories.

TinyStories ([Eldan & Li, 2023](#bib.bib13)) is a corpus of short
synthetic stories in simple English. We tokenize it with our own
byte-pair-encoding (BPE) tokenizer of $`V=1024`$ tokens, trained on the
corpus, and hold one story per sequence of $`L=512`$: the story tokens,
an EOS token, and PAD tokens up to $`L`$. We keep the train and
validation splits of the released corpus and drop the 3.9% of training
and 3.6% of validation stories that do not fit. This leaves 2,611,361
training stories and 26,637 validation stories, which we split evenly
into validation and test sets. During training, we corrupt and attend to
padding like any other token but never score it, so the model does not
learn where a story ends. We therefore sample at a known length: each
sample takes the padding positions of a validation story, and these
positions follow the forward bridge
$`q_{s\mid t,0}(\cdot\mid Z_{t}^{i},\texttt{PAD})`$ from the prior down
to $`t_{1}`$ instead of being shown clean, so the model sees them as it
did in training.

#### OpenWebText.

OpenWebText ([Gokaslan & Cohen, 2019](#bib.bib18)) is an open
reproduction of the WebText corpus. We tokenize it with our own BPE
tokenizer of $`V=1024`$ tokens, trained on the corpus, and pack
documents into sequences of $`L=1024`$. We wrap each document in BOS and
EOS tokens, follow it with a uniformly random number of 0 to 127 PAD
tokens, and cut the resulting stream into consecutive sequences of $`L`$
tokens, so a sequence can hold several documents or part of one, and we
do not mask attention between documents. As for TinyStories, we corrupt
and attend to padding but never score it, and we exclude it from the
likelihoods and the decoded text of
App. [F.3](#A6.SS3 "F.3 Evaluation ‣ Appendix F Experimental details ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks").
The corpus has no official split, so we hold out a random 100k documents
before packing and split them evenly into validation and test sets,
which keeps the three sets document-disjoint. Like Text8, we sample it
unconditionally.

Table [11](#A6.T11 "Table 11 ‣ OpenWebText. ‣ F.6 Language modeling ‣ Appendix F Experimental details ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks")
gives, at the validation-selected setting of each kernel, the pooled
entropy, MAUVE, and GenPPL, together with the held-out NELBO of
App. [F.3](#A6.SS3.SSS0.Px1 "NELBO. ‣ F.3 Evaluation ‣ Appendix F Experimental details ‣ Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-SetDiffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks"),
which does not depend on the sampler.
````
